articles.title_orig: Crypto platform Webull is getting slammed over its alleged China ties
articles.title_zh: Crypto platform Webull is getting slammed over its alleged China ties
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Webull, the crypto trading platform that has faced scrutiny over its alleged China ties, have tanked nearly 76% since it went public through a special acquisition corporation early last year – but that should hardly be a surprise if you read On The Money.Shares of Webull, the crypto trading platform that has faced scrutiny over its alleged China ties, have tanked nearly 76% since it went public through a special acquisition corporation early last year – but that should hardly be a surprise if you read On The Money.
Since at least 2023 , this column has been reporting growing concern in Congress over whether management of the discount broker with 28 million users worldwide is too cozy with the Chinese surveillance state . The worry is that the firm collects sensitive customer data on Americans that could be shared with Chinese spies–something the company has steadfastly denied.
On Wednesday, the bipartisan House Select Committee on China put a finer point on those concerns in a 23-page report titled “Free Trades, Hidden Ties Exposing Webull’s China Links.”
According to the report, “Webull’s ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People’s Republic of China,” also referred to as the PRC in the paper.
Webull in the past has described itself as “both a US and Chinese company,” and has argued that its American customer data is stored in the US and is 100% secure from foreigners. But the report notes that a Chinese national, Anquan Wang, is Webull’s founder, chairman and CEO.
The report also notes that Wang controls the company through a dual-class share structure with 79.2% of the company’s voting power, meaning Wang can “control the election of directors and other major corporate decisions requiring shareholder approval.”
The Committee said its findings underscore “national security concerns” that have escalated in recent years, where among other issues, “Webull’s data practices expose American investors to PRC legal and surveillance risk.”
As i mentioned, the allegation that Webull is a tool for espionage is something the company has always denied. It repeated its denial after the explosive report took shares down 20% when it first hit the tape Wednesday morning. Webull finished the day down 19%, trading at $5.89 at the market’s close.
In a statement to On The Money, a Webull press rep says “It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull.”
The Webull press rep didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on what those inaccuracies were.
The statement added, “Webull has made every effort to cooperate with the Committee, but did not hear from them for more than 20 months before this report was released. Webull’s US business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Fla., and its office in New York City, while US customer data is stored in the US and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the US. We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide.”
A  spokesman for the committee, formally known as the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party chaired by John Moolenaar (R-MI), tells On The Money that in regards to the company’s data storage the “report does not dispute where the data is stored. Its finding is about who can reach the data and the systems that process it.”
The US securities markets are regulated by the SEC or the Securities and Exchange Commission, a federal agency also known as Wall Street’s top cop given its importance in monitoring Wall Street. FINRA, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, is the securities industry’s self-regulator, which under law provides front-line oversight of Wall Street and its various players. Indeed, Webull appears in compliance with both outfits. A press rep for FINRA declined to comment; an SEC spokesman had no immediate comment.
The report, meanwhile, touts six so-called findings: “Webull’s data practices expose American investors to PRC legal and surveillance risk; Webull misrepresented where key employees worked and how they were supervised; Webull’s governance is dominated by PRC-linked control: Webull’s regulatory controls were weaker than its assurances suggested; Webull’s subsidiary accepted PRC government funding conditional on CCP loyalty while its affiliates expanded in China; Webull’s clearing and custody safeguards are concerning.”
Sign up to receive On The Money by Charlie Gasparino in your inbox every Thursday.
It is calling for various reforms including the extension of “foreign adversary data protections to brokerage records.”
The report’s concerns echo some of the issues US regulators have grappled with when charting the future of the popular formerly China-owned short-video app TikTok. That includes worries that the PRC government, namely the Chinese Communist Party, is siphoning user data for espionage purposes since the surveillance state there basically controls every company on its soil.
Both Republicans and Democrats have debated for years whether to ban TikTok, worried about the potential for identity theft, the CCP gleaning “biometric identifiers” and search history of its 170 million US users.
President Trump, who once sought to ban the app, recently cut a deal with China in which its US subsidiary is now majority owned by US investors and data is held in the so-called cloud operated by US tech giant Oracle.

articles.title_orig: Saudi authorities say 3 killed in Houthi-claimed attacks on Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: Saudi authorities say 3 killed in Houthi-claimed attacks on Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
Three Saudi Arabian nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said, after Yemen's Houthis said they had targeted the facility.
The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X.
It added that the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second had struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia.
One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement.
Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said.
Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two ballistic missiles.
The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks.
The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.
Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport in Riyadh.
The latest attacks come amid mark an escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.
The Houthi military spokesman said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" that saw "60 air strikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".
The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.
But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

articles.title_orig: Commentary: The story China wants you to swallow
articles.title_zh: Commentary: The story China wants you to swallow
articles.content_orig:
On May 22, 2018, China Central Television broadcast a glowing segment about salmon farming in western China. Over images of sleek fish cutting through clear water, the narrator marveled that “a precious fish like salmon, which typically lives in the open ocean,” could now be raised in the desert. Technology had made the improbable possible. “The land is the same land, and the people are the same people,” the program declared, “but when technology is brought in, miracles are born.”
Viewers were unconvinced and immediately began voicing skepticism about seafood coming from such a surprising place. Within days, Chinese social-media users questioned whether the fish on screen was actually salmon at all. “People expect Atlantic salmon, but we’re getting freshwater rainbow trout that costs half as much,” one Beijing-based WeChat account complained. “How could you not be angry?” The science writer Fang Shimin put it bluntly: “This is cheap rainbow trout being passed off as expensive salmon.”
Where the media campaign had hoped to tell a bigger and more hopeful story about the success of farming in a place most people thought was impossible, the public reaction veered in a different direction. China has rapidly expanded its fish farms in its historically restive and inland west—erecting more than 1,000 in Tibet and Xinjiang—motivated by a slate of priorities including food security, settling a nomadic and politically volatile population, poverty alleviation, and reducing fishing pressure on its polluted eastern shores.
The state-led media campaign around China’s desert seafood also sought to redirect Western attention away from human rights abuses that are pervasive in these two Chinese regions. The growth of these farms in China’s west is the focus of a sweeping investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project , a news organization in Washington, DC, which showed how much seafood from Xinjiang is reaching the U.S., including government facilities, in violation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act.
The backlash over rainbow trout was not only about unfair prices, but also about questions of food safety. In a 2018 interview with China Daily, food safety expert Zhong Kai reacted to Chinese companies advertising salmon that was actually trout. He advised that eating freshwater trout raw, as one would eat salmon, could lead to serious illness.
China’s aquaculture industry has expanded at staggering speed, and with that expansion have come the familiar pressures of industrial animal farming: crowding, disease, waste, and chemical intervention. Chinese researchers have increasingly found illegal quantities of drugs in farmed fish, including antibiotics and sedatives at levels that threaten humans.
These food safety questions are relevant outside of China. One company, called Xinjiang Tianyun Organic Agriculture, now ships to 14 countries, including the U.S., where its products are sold at Walmart and served at American schools, prisons, and military bases. This trade occurs in violation of a U.S. ban on goods produced in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region, which Congress enacted in 2021 after finding human rights abuses to be pervasive and severe there. Tianyun’s seafood reaches the U.S. by way of supplier deals with Aqua Star and Sysco, according to Bait to Plate , an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.
Tianyun said in a statement that claims of systemic forced labor “are completely factually unfounded” and described the U.S. ban as unreasonable and politically motivated. The company added that it strictly abides by China’s laws on labor and contracts. Aqua Star did not reply to a request for comment. Walmart confirmed that it sources seafood from Aqua Star. Sysco said it expects its suppliers to follow all U.S., international, and local laws and that they suspend contracts when they do not.
The Chinese efforts to promote seafood from Xinjiang are not new. As early as 2011, Vice Minister of Agriculture Niu Dun urged officials to “enhance brand building and awareness of the market expansion of Xinjiang’s seafood enterprises.” A 2017 government action plan instructed local offices to coordinate with mainstream media to “systematically publicize the progress of fishery poverty alleviation” in Xinjiang, fostering “an environment of positive public opinion.”
This marketing push intensified in August 2023 when there was a sharp spike in social media posts on the topic. The hashtag “No joke—Xinjiang really does produce seafood” climbed Weibo’s Hot Search List. Videos associated with “Xinjiang seafood” amassed millions of views. Soon, the theme leapt beyond China’s own internet. YouTube, which is banned in China, saw a sharp rise in Xinjiang seafood videos that fall.
“All signs point to this being a coordinated campaign,” said Fergus Ryan, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. He explained that it had unusual speed and reach due to top-down and algorithmic amplification, unlike natural viral events, which typically grow slowly through grassroots sharing. In his view, the campaign served to redirect attention from mounting international scrutiny after a 2023 investigation found that seafood plants in Shandong had used thousands of Xinjiang labor transfers to process fish destined for major Western markets. Against that backdrop, Ryan argued, the upbeat Xinjiang seafood videos functioned as a kind of information flooding, crowding search and recommendation systems with stories of “fishery miracles” rather than forced labor.
China is using other tactics to prevent companies from insulating themselves from these sorts of human rights abuses. In April 2026, the government announced new rules that would make it even more difficult for multinationals to conduct due diligence on supply chains in industries like seafood and cotton.
Part of the same effort, the Chinese government has also organized media tours for foreign reporters and actively recruited foreign food buffs—called vloggers or “frontier influencers”—to record and post videos and other testimonials about the wonders of growing fish in Xinjiang.
Among the most popular frontier influencers is a Russian student named Melissa. “Today, we’ve come to a salmon farm in Nilka, Xinjiang, to be an employee for a day and see what it’s like for ourselves,” she said in a video published in September 2025. These videos were amplified by media outlets affiliated with the government, as well as on state-run channels on YouTube and Facebook. A video featuring Jack, an American vlogger, showcased his tour of a fish farm on the edge of the desert. “It’s incredible how they have developed such a barren land to this extent,” he narrated.
But it is the government itself that attempts to frame the unlikely industry it has engineered in Xinjiang in the grandest terms. In a 2025 article published by state media, Xinjiang’s aquaculture hotbed in the deserts and rivers of its forbidding western frontier was declared “a testament to human ingenuity and resilience.”
“Xinjiang’s aquaculture is not merely about producing fish,” the article went on, “it is about reimagining how inland regions can contribute to the nation’s protein security, how technology can redefine agriculture, and how harmony between people and nature can be sustained in the most challenging of environments. From snow-fed rivers to desert oases, Xinjiang has shown that blue dreams can indeed flourish on dry land.”
This commentary is based on reporting for a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.
The Outlaw Ocean Project is a non-profit journalism organization based in Washington D.C. that produces investigative stories about human rights, labor, and environmental concerns.
The views expressed here are their own and do not reflect the position of RFA.

articles.title_orig: EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war
articles.title_zh: EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war
articles.content_orig:
Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné says bloc will support 46 strategic projects including lithium and rare earths plants
The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China , the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects.
Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc.
“We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.”
The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn).
They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China , with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.
“We’re pulling out all the stops to move as quickly as possible. The primary objective is the targets set by law, and beyond that, there’s a geopolitical challenge that could catch up with us very quickly,” said Séjourné.
“Mines are opening, factories are being built, financing agreements are being signed, and a European value chain is emerging,” Séjourné added.
Amid some scepticism over the EU’s ability to meet its 2030 targets to reduce dependencies on China, Séjourné cited three “emblematic” projects which have previously been identified as strategic, earmarking them for accelerated permits.
These included a rare earths plant near Pau in south-western France. The Carester plant, which is expected to be up and running in late 2026, produces dysprosium and terbium, “two raw materials for which we are almost entirely dependent on China”, used in magnets for electric vehicles and offshore wind turbines.
“This single project could account for about 15% of global production of these oxides. That is no small feat,” Séjourné said.
He also name-checked a gallium plant in Greece which is already up and running.
The third, Keliber, a lithium extraction and processing plant in Finland, is also operational after €150m support from the European Investment Bank.
The 46 projects are the second batch of initiatives to receive flagship status since the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024, which legally mandates the European Commission to reduce the bloc’s dependency on foreign countries.

The EU hopes to follow in the footsteps of Japan, which has reduced dependency on China for rare earths to 60% from 90% since 2011, when Beijing prohibited exports of about 20 entities to Japan, claiming they were being used for military purposes.
Although the flagship status does not bring the projects direct funds, it enables accelerated permitting, and help in mobilising funds.
However, there has been criticism in industry within the EU that the scheme is not strong enough to deliver targets to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the bloc’s needs by 2030.
The French lithium refiner Viridian Lithium, which received EU strategic status in 2025, went into judicial liquidation in March this year.
Earlier this year, a group of 23 of the 60 projects designated strategic in 2025 wrote to the European Commission calling for more action to “urgently unlock projects, particularly those working towards final investment decision which face acute liquidity and market pressure and ​immediate jeopardy”.
Séjourné said member states had unlocked €1bn for six of the projects, with the European Investment Bank providing another €660m for eight projects.

articles.title_orig: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
articles.title_zh: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African legal pioneer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for defending international law and institutions in a world in which increasingly “might overtakes right.”
Pillay, 85, has a decadeslong career that spans defending Nelson Mandela and standing up against the racist apartheid regime in South Africa, to leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Using the award to make a wider point about geopolitics, Frydnes contrasted Pillay’s work with the wider international “shift towards power politics,” in which “international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”
Her “distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” he said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”
Pillay learned of her prize at the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany. She told an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” prompting laughter.
That was a reference to President Donald Trump’s long-standing ambitions to win the Nobel Peace Prize, and the offer by last year’s winner, Maria Corina Machado, to share it with him as she sought support for her efforts in Venezuela.
“Everybody asks me: ‘When are you going to stop? When are you going to stop?’” Pillay said , adding that despite turning 85 last month, she had no intention of doing so.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza, namely what’s happening there is genocide,” she said to cheers.
“One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage,” she added. “But why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law and you look at all the facts.”
Having just been told the news, she added jokingly, “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”
Among her many positions, Pillay has been a judge on the  International Criminal Court
Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, was in Germany and among the first people to congratulate Pillay.
“This could not be a better choice at a time of attacks against international justice,” Callamard told NBC News. “She is a former ICC judge at a time when the U.S. administration is seeking to destroy the ICC,” and she led the U.N. commission “which found that Israel committed the crime of genocide at a time when many states are trying to defend and protect Israel’s actions.”
Pillay was not among those speculated to be front-runners, who included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, and Mykola Kuleba , who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly taken to Russia.
The Norwegian Nobel Institute said it had has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize, with politicians, international judges and professors among those who can put names forward. The committee that decides the winner is composed of five members appointed by the Norwegian Parliament.
The leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia all said they nominated Trump for the prize, though he said this week he didn’t think he would win.
“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said in the Oval Office Wednesday. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”
Alexander Smith is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: India Selected to Host WTTC Global Summit 2027, the World’s Most Important Tourism Event
articles.title_zh: India Selected to Host WTTC Global Summit 2027, the World’s Most Important Tourism Event
articles.content_orig:
The World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) today announced that India will host the WTTC Global Summit in 2027, bringing the world’s leading Travel & Tourism CEOs and government leaders to Delhi as the country’s tourism sector enters a new era of growth and global opportunity, supported by one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing domestic travel markets.
As the sector’s most important global event, the WTTC Global Summit attracts the highest level of public and private sector participation from across the world. India was selected following a highly competitive process involving 22 destinations that expressed interest in hosting the event.
The 2027 Summit will provide a global platform to showcase India’s extraordinary tourism offering, the strength of its domestic visitor economy, and its growing appeal to international travellers, while bringing together the public and private sectors to address the opportunities and challenges shaping the future of Travel & Tourism.
The announcement comes during the WTTC Global Summit in Malta, where H.E. Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Union Minister of Tourism and Culture, Government of India, participated in discussions on the future of the sector and has been recognised with a WTTC Global Champion Award for his leadership and contribution to Travel & Tourism.
India has emerged as one of the world’s fastest-growing Travel & Tourism economies. According to WTTC’s latest Economic Impact Research, the sector contributed US$263.6 billion to India’s economy in 2025, growing by 7.3% and supporting 46.2 million jobs – more than one in every ten jobs in the country.
The momentum is expected to continue. WTTC forecasts that Travel & Tourism’s contribution to India’s economy will grow by 8.5% in 2026, reaching US$286.1 billion, while supporting 48.1 million jobs. Over the next decade, the sector is projected to almost double in economic size, reaching US$527 billion by 2036.
India’s enormous domestic tourism market provides a powerful foundation for this growth. Domestic visitor spending reached US$203 billion in 2025, accounting for 86% of total Travel & Tourism spending, while international visitor spending represents a significant opportunity for further expansion.
WTTC’s research projects that India will move from being the world’s 10th-largest Travel & Tourism economy to fourth by 2036, underlining the scale of the opportunity ahead. International visitor spending is also forecast to grow significantly over the coming decade, highlighting the potential for India to capture a greater share of global tourism demand.
The country’s scale, diverse tourism offering and expanding infrastructure are creating opportunities across leisure, business travel, hospitality, aviation, technology, investment and destination development. The 2027 Summit will provide a unique opportunity for international businesses and investors to engage directly with India and explore partnerships across its rapidly developing tourism ecosystem.
Manfredi Lefebvre d'Ovidio, Chairman, WTTC, said : “ We are delighted to bring the world’s most important Travel & Tourism event to India in 2027, chosen from among 22 destinations. Delhi will provide the perfect stage for global leaders to come together, drive collaboration, and continue shaping the future of the sector. ”
Gloria Guevara, President & CEO, WTTC, said : “ India is a country with extraordinary tourism potential and a sector that is already delivering remarkable economic growth. Its scale, ambition and growing global connectivity make it a natural place to bring the world’s Travel & Tourism leaders together.
This will be an opportunity to showcase the country to our global membership, strengthen public-private partnerships and look at how India can capture even more of the international demand that is driving the next chapter of global Travel & Tourism. ”
The decision to bring the Global Summit to India follows a period of significant expansion for the country’s Travel & Tourism sector and reflects WTTC’s commitment to bringing its flagship event to markets that are helping shape the future of the industry.
India has already demonstrated the strength of its domestic tourism market, while the next phase of growth will increasingly focus on expanding its international visitor economy. WTTC’s research highlights the opportunity to build on India’s strong domestic foundation and attract a greater share of international visitor spending.
The announcement also reinforces the importance of strong collaboration between governments and the private sector. WTTC’s Global Summit brings together the leaders responsible for investment, infrastructure, connectivity, hospitality, aviation, technology and destination development, creating a unique environment for new partnerships and investment opportunities.
– ENDS – For more information about WTTC, please visit wttc.org For media enquiries, please contact Paul Charles / Philip Allport / Rob Morris at The PC Agency via [email protected]
About the World Travel & Tourism Council
The World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) is the global body representing the private sector of Travel & Tourism and the leading authority on the sector’s economic and social contribution worldwide. Its members include Chairmen, Presidents and CEOs of the world’s leading travel and tourism companies across hotels, airlines, airports, cruise lines, tour operators, technology platforms and destinations, spanning every major region globally.
WTTC works to advance sustainable growth across the Travel & Tourism sector by driving collaboration between industry leaders and governments, shaping global policy, and providing authoritative research on the sector’s economic impact worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Calidore String Quartet Performs World Premiere of Anna Clyne’s The Seven Ravens
articles.title_zh: Calidore String Quartet Performs World Premiere of Anna Clyne’s The Seven Ravens
articles.content_orig:
The Calidore String Quartet will give the world premiere of Anna Clyne’s The Seven Ravens at Konserthuset Stockholm on 10 October . Co-commissioned by Konserthuset Stockholm, Shriver Hall Concert Series and The Phillips Collection, the work will also feature on a forthcoming album of Clyne’s complete chamber works, to be released on Signum Records. The Stockholm programme pairs Clyne’s new work with Dvořák’s String Quartet No. 12, “The American” , and Korngold’s String Quartet No. 3.
The quartet will give the US premiere of The Seven Ravens at Baltimore’s Shriver Hall in May 2027 . The programme will also include Haydn’s String Quartet in D major, Caroline Shaw’s Entr’acte and Beethoven’s String Quartet in B-flat major.
Elsewhere in the 2026/27 season, the Calidore String Quartet will tour extensively across North America, with engagements at New York’s Lincoln Center and in Montreal and Portland, a tour of California, and a Beethoven residency in Denver. In Europe, the quartet returns to Amsterdam, London’s Wigmore Hall and Padova.

Occupied chinstrap nests on Zavodovski Island have fallen by 63% since 2011, scientists say, with warming seas pushing the penguins' krill prey out of reach
The world’s largest penguin colony has lost its title after a steep decline in chinstrap penguins on a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, according to new research by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
The study, published in the journal Current Biology, found that the number of occupied chinstrap nests on Zavodovski Island, in the South Sandwich Islands, fell by 63% between 2011 and 2025. The island now has the highest rate of chinstrap decline anywhere in the world, and the title of largest colony passes to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea, more than 5,000km away.
In 2011, Zavodovski was home to an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said Prof Norman Ratcliffe, the BAS penguin ecologist who led the research.
The researchers say the cause is climate-driven change in the Southern Ocean. Chinstraps have a specialist diet and prefer cooler water, and tracking data showed they forage to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill. As the water warms, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
“Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food,” Ratcliffe said.
The island’s macaroni penguins, which have a broader diet and can switch to fish and crustaceans when krill become scarce, increased by 28% between 2011 and 2016 and have been stable since. Tracking data showed them foraging in warmer waters to the north-east. Ratcliffe described the shift as the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica.

The team travelled for 15 days by yacht to reach the island, which is more than 2,000km from the nearest permanent human settlement. They used drone surveys, aerial photography from an RAF aircraft based in the Falklands, and tracking devices fitted to penguins.
The scientists ruled out several other explanations. Zavodovski’s volcano, Mount Curry, erupted in March 2016, but the decline began years earlier and has been steady, and the researchers say it is not to blame. They also dismissed competition between the two penguin species for nesting space, and krill fishing, because harvesting is banned in the marine protected area surrounding the island. However, it is unclear how krill fishing in areas connected by currents to the protected area might be affecting wider food supplies.
The South Sandwich Islands hold around 30% of the world’s chinstrap population. The researchers say the declines here, together with those elsewhere in Antarctica, could tip the species into the “Endangered” category on the IUCN Red List.
Ratcliffe warned that the loss of chinstraps could have wider consequences for marine food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely,” he told the Guardian.
Peter Fretwell, a BAS researcher who specialises in remote sensing of penguins, said the findings showed that even the most remote places were affected by climate change. “Not even they can escape the impacts of climate change,” he said.
The study comes six months after emperor penguins were declared an endangered species because of sea ice loss.

Live updates: Hurricane Isaias threatens the Gulf Coast with dangerous landfall expected tonight
Double red flags are flying across Orange Beach, Alabama today as dangerous, life-threatening surf and powerful rip currents surge ahead of Hurricane Isaias.
We are just minutes away from the National Hurricane Center’s full 11 a.m. ET advisory.
This advisory will deliver updated central pressure readings, revised maximum sustained wind speeds, an updated forecast track cone, and official watch/warning adjustments across the Gulf Coast.
Our team of meteorologists is standing by to analyze the newly released coordinates, intensity trends, and storm surge grids, and we will break down all the vital updates and local impacts right here in real-time as soon as the data hits.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis addressed residents today regarding the threat posed by Hurricane Isaias as the major Category 3 storm rapidly approaches landfall along Florida's Big Bend and Panhandle regions.
Emphasizing the storm's dangerous combination of major winds, life-threatening storm surge, and torrential rainfall, DeSantis urged all Floridians in the path to remain vigilant, heed local evacuation warnings, and stay acutely aware of rapidly changing conditions.
State emergency management teams and National Guard assets remain fully pre-positioned to assist local communities as the core of the storm moves ashore.
Pensacola Beach Lifeguards/Facebook
Emergency officials have ordered the immediate evacuation of Pensacola Beach, with lifeguards flying double red flags to signal that the Gulf is strictly closed to all water activities.
Heavy surf is already building past 6 feet, creating life-threatening rip currents as tropical force conditions accelerate toward the shore.
Lifeguards are officially clearing remaining visitors from the sand and heading off Pensacola Beach.
All residents and visitors are urged to pack up, move inland immediately, and stay completely out of the surf as dangerous coastal conditions deteriorate.
Exclusive analysis from FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist Bryan Norcross
Hurricane Isaias has intensified into a well-developed Category 3 hurricane and is making its move toward the Gulf Coast.
Thankfully, the upper-level winds are somewhat hostile, or it would have gotten a lot stronger like Milton did two years ago.
The peak winds will likely decrease a bit later today as the system approaches landfall, but it won't change the impacts significantly.
Damaging winds, storm surge, and rain heavy enough to cause flooding will affect the entire Florida Panhandle beginning late this afternoon, peaking this evening.
Early today is the last chance to maneuver before the weather starts deteriorating this afternoon.
Overnight, strong winds, which will likely knock out power, and torrential rain will spread into Alabama, Georgia, and eastern Mississippi.
Tornadoes will also be a threat in the outer bands north and well east of Isaias's center, including Tallahassee, North Florida, and into Georgia.
The El Niño-driven jet stream ripping across the south will morph the storm into something of a comma shape. The worst weather is likely to be ahead of the center of circulation and in the tail of the comma well to the east.
The jet stream will energize torrential rain, and tornadoes are possible in both the head and tail of the storm as it moves inland.
Strong wind gusts are likely over a wide area, including the entire State of Alabama and most of Georgia, especially near and to the east of where the center of Isaias tracks.
Bad weather will arrive well in advance of the center, which will cross the coast mid to late evening on the current schedule.
Thunderstorms are likely along the I-10 corridor this afternoon with the worst weather arriving in the evening.
The threat of heavy rain and tornadoes will continue through the night and into tomorrow as the comma-shaped hurricane pushes north.
The hurricane will merge with a large upper-level low-pressure system to spread tropical moisture across the Southeast.
The combo system will draw moisture from the Atlantic as well as the Gulf, elevating the flood threat along the Carolina coast in addition to higher elevations well inland. Stay aware of flood alerts issued for your area.
Isaias will push Gulf water over the coast along a large portion of the northern Gulf. The National Hurricane Center is forecasting the tide to be up to 7 feet above normal height around the time of landfall.
That assumes that landfall occurs around high tide time. If the tide is lower, obviously the impact would be a bit diminished, but there isn't much tidal swing on the northern Gulf beaches.
Tomorrow is a big football Saturday across the Southeast. If you are attending a game, consider carefully before getting on the road. Trees might be down, power might be out, and flooding rain is likely in some areas.
Isaias is now close enough for Doppler radar to show the storm's eye
NEXRAD Doppler radar sites along the northern Gulf Coast are now painting the inner structure of Hurricane Isaias, with the storm’s eye coming distinctly into radar range as the system closes the distance toward the shore.
Radar loops show the well-defined eyewall wrapping thick bands of torrential rain and high wind near the center, giving meteorologists continuous, high-resolution tracking of the storm's exact position and movement.
As the eye advances closer to the coast over the coming hours, the National Hurricane Center will begin providing hourly status updates as landfall nears.
Radar shows heavy rain approaching the coast with wind speeds ramping up
Outer wind bands are beginning to make their presence felt along the northern Gulf Coast this morning, with observation sites already logging gusts approaching 30 mph.
These early squalls mark the leading edge of the storm's expansive wind field, and speeds will steadily build throughout the day as the system moves closer.
Latest Risk Of Weather Impact (ROWI) forecast for South Carolina vs. Florida
As tropical rainbands push inland, several college football matchups across the Southeast are facing a High ROWI (Risk Of Weather Impact) rating for Saturday’s game slate.
Downpours, gusty winds, and the threat of lightning delays will make ball security and footing a major factor, forcing teams to lean heavily on their ground games as conditions deteriorate.
Fans heading to stadiums across the impact zone should prepare for wet tailgating, potential game delays, and slick stadium concourses throughout the afternoon.
Latest Risk Of Weather Impact (ROWI) forecast for Duke vs. Georgia Tech
The FOX Forecast Center warns that widespread, long-duration power outages will surge across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama as high winds and tropical squalls batter the region through Saturday.
Latest power outage forecast from FOX Weather
Tropical downpours saturating the ground combined with damaging sustained winds will easily uproot trees and bring down utility lines across the core impact zone.
Residents in these communities should prepare for potentially extended grid failures by securing emergency power sources, charging necessary devices, and finalizing shelter preparations before conditions reach their peak.
As the storm moves ashore, the FOX Forecast Center warns of a rising risk of fast-moving tornadoes spinning up within outer rainbands across North Florida and into Georgia later today through Saturday.
Tornado threat extends north and east on Saturday as Isaias spreads out
Tornadoes are extremely common in landfalling tropical systems because low-level friction over land slows surface winds while stronger winds aloft keep moving quickly, creating intense vertical wind shear.
This dramatic change in wind speed and direction with height tilts and rotates localized updrafts inside outer squalls, producing short-lived spin-ups that can form with little to no advance warning.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia says it must defend itself against Eritrea's 'all-out invasion'
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia says it must defend itself against Eritrea's 'all-out invasion'
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.
Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

articles.title_orig: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
articles.title_zh: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
articles.content_orig:
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
A Defence Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," said Hegseth.
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.
The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers in a crowded medical building at Fort Hood.
Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who was shot seven times in the attack, told the BBC's Today programme that he supported the execution by firing squad, as a method "befitting" for what he did.
He does not believe everyone should be able to watch the livestream, concerned about the message it sends younger people, but says it is important that those affected by the shooting are given the opportunity.
"As far as the families of the fallen and the families of the survivors, and the survivors themselves, yes, I think we should be able to look at it uncensored."
Lunsford says he plans to attend the execution and before they pull the trigger he wants Hasan to look him in the eyes. "I want him to know he failed. I'm still here."
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
A Pentagon spokesperson said on Monday that Trump had approved the defence secretary's recommendation. The BBC has asked the White House whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly.
Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
In court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgement on its legality to move forward.
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution.
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened.
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says.
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-restricted.
Only certain categories of people, such as journalists and relatives, are permitted to watch military executions under Army Regulation 190-55 . People aged under 18 are excluded.
The BBC has asked the Pentagon and US Army if the rules restricting who can watch will be waived and what safeguards will be in place to stop young people from watching the stream.
A Defence Department official told the BBC that more details on the livestreamed execution would follow.
The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.
Donald Trump overturned Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions when he returned to the White House.
According to Pew Research conducted in July , two thirds of Americans (66%) support executions for murder, a figure which has risen six points in the last five years.
The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of World War Two.

articles.title_orig: BIDMC Researchers Conduct First Real-World Study of Safety and Quality of Patient-Facing AI in Primary Care
articles.title_zh: BIDMC Researchers Conduct First Real-World Study of Safety and Quality of Patient-Facing AI in Primary Care
articles.content_orig:
BOSTON — The aging population, workforce changes, and patients’ increasingly complex medical needs are all factors straining primary care systems around the world. Artificial intelligence tools have emerged as a potential means of extending the capabilities of health care workers, including in primary care settings. Large language models (LLMs), also known as chatbots, have performed extremely well in simulations. However, little is known about how these systems perform with real patients.
Researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) have conducted what they believe is the first prospective real-world study of a patient-facing conversational AI system in primary care, taking an important step toward evaluating the technology through the same kind of rigorous clinical testing used for other health care interventions. The findings appear in The Lancet .
“Despite the theoretical performance of patient-facing AI in experimental settings, it is unclear how conversationally safe these encounters are in a real-world setting," said Adam Rodman, MD, Director of AI Programs at the Carl J. Shapiro Institute for Research and Education at BIDMC. "Before we begin evaluating them as workload interventions, AI tools must first be shown to operate safely and acceptably in real care workflows. With this research, we set out to assess whether this kind of technology could improve both patient and physician experience."
Rodman and colleagues in collaboration with researchers at Google evaluated the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE), a medical AI chatbot that patients used from home after scheduling an urgent primary care appointment with a BIDMC physician. Through a secure text-chat interface, the system asked patients about their symptoms, gathered medical histories, provided possible diagnoses for patients to review with their doctor, and generated a summary for clinician review prior to the visit.
Conducted between April and November 2025, the study enrolled 114 patients, 98 of whom completed both the AI interaction and their primary care appointment. Every conversation was monitored in real time by a board-certified internal medicine physician who could intervene if a patient appeared at risk of harm, experienced significant emotional distress, asked to end the session, or if the physician identified a potential safety concern — such as the need to clarify symptoms, provide emergency care instructions, or address concern about a serious possible diagnosis.
Across all 98 completed encounters, none of the conversations required a safety-stop intervention. Supervising physicians identified one hallucination and provided additional clinical clarification in five cases.
"This study helps establish the baseline characteristics of such real-world conversations,” said co-first author Peter Brodeur, MD, a clinical fellow in cardiovascular medicine at BIDMC. “These baseline characteristics provide a foundation for all future prospective trials aimed at discovering when human-on-the-loop workflows may be appropriate.”
Patients appeared receptive to the technology. Patients rated the quality of AMIE's conversations favorably — as did physician evaluators — across most measures. Moreover, patient attitudes toward AI improved after interacting with the chatbot and remained elevated following their appointment with a clinician.
"One of the most important questions was simply how patients would engage with a conversational AI system in a real clinical setting," said co-first author Jacob Koshy, MD, MPH, a hospitalist in the Division of General Medicine at BIDMC. "By prospectively observing these interactions, we were able to better understand both the opportunities and the limitations of the technology in the context of routine patient care."
While patients gave high marks to the system's ability to listen, explain information, and help them feel at ease, concerns remained around two areas: trust in the confidentiality of information shared with the system and trust in the chatbot's honesty and trustworthiness. Researchers said those findings underscore the importance of continued work to build patient trust as AI tools move into clinical care.
"Research suggests that patient trust in medical AI systems flows from relationships with their human providers," said Rodman. "Future research will need to explore which interaction characteristics can build patient trust and how AI interactions can enhance the patient-physician relationship."
The findings also suggest the technology may have practical value in clinical workflows.
Primary care providers were able to review an AI-generated transcript or summary before seeing their patients for 44 cases. In 75 percent of cases, physicians said doing so helped them prepare for the visit and in 57 percent of cases, they reported it may have influenced their clinical approach. In only one case did a provider report the interaction as somewhat harmful, citing concern that a patient may have experienced anxiety after AMIE included lymphoma among its possible diagnoses.
Rodman and colleagues emphasized that the study was designed to evaluate feasibility rather than to determine whether AI improves health outcomes.
“Our primary care practice — and our hospital — has a long history of rigorously monitoring the safety of the clinical care we provide, and this study serves as an exemplar of how the safety of AI may be assessed prior to clinical implementation,” said co-senior author Marc L. Cohen, MD, Clinical Chief of Primary Care, Division of General Medicine at BIDMC. “We believe the future involves continued involvement of human clinicians in patient care, but see a future where the triad of patient, human clinician, and AI help to provide our patients with the very best evidenced-based care possible," said Cohen.
Co-authors included Ava Homiar, BS; Charles Wu, MD; Hannah M. Ferrera, MD; Lindsey Crowley, MD; Christine G. Kohn, MD; Vinay Kadiyala, MD; Wendy Du, MD; David Feinbloom, MD; Jonathan X. Li, MD; Spencer E. Rittner, MD; and Rob Fields, MD of BIDMC; Selena K. Zhang, BS, of Harvard Medical School; Anil Palepu, PhD; Roma Ruparel, MPH; Joseph Xu, PhD; Amy Wang, MD; Jihyeon Lee, MS; Ellery Wulczyn, MS; Kavita Kulkarni, MS; Jessica M. Williams, BS; Renee Wong, BEcom; Petar Sirkovic, PhD; Alessio Orlandi, PhD; Christopher Semturs, MS; Yun Liu, PhD; Juraj Gottweis, MS; Dale R. Webster, PhD; Katherine Chou, MS; Avinatan Hassidim, PhD; Yossi Matias, PhD; James Manyika, DPhil; and Mike Schaekermann, PhD, of Google Research; and Khaled Saab, PhD; Ryutaro Tanno, PhD; David Stutz, PhD; Wei-Hung Weng, MD; David Barrett, PhD; Elahe Vedadi, PhD; S. Sara Mahdavi, PhD; Tao Tu, PhD; Joëlle Barral, PhD; Pushmeet Kohli, PhD; Vivek Natarajan, MS; and Alan Karthikesalingam, PhD, of Google DeepMind.
This study was funded by Alphabet. Adam Rodman, MD, served as a visiting researcher at Google during part of the study. Full disclosures are available in the published manuscript.

BIDMC is a teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School, and consistently ranks as a national leader among independent hospitals in National Institutes of Health funding. BIDMC is the official hospital of the Boston Red Sox.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center is a part of Beth Israel Lahey Health , a healthcare system that brings together academic medical centers and teaching hospitals, community and specialty hospitals, more than 4,700 physicians and 39,000 employees in a shared mission to expand access to great care and advance the science and practice of medicine through groundbreaking research and education.

articles.content_orig:
New FDX Fusion platform extends GF’s FD-SOI leadership as the first process technology in Europe to deliver single-digit nanometer digital performance optimized for the physical world
DRESDEN, Germany, Oct. 9, 2026 – GlobalFoundries (Nasdaq: GFS) (GF) today unveiled plans for its new FDX Fusion ™ FD-SOI platform, purpose-built for the evolving requirements of Physical AI. Designed to be the world’s most advanced FD-SOI technology, FDX Fusion will bring leading features and performance for the unique requirements of STAC (Sense, Think, Act, Communicate) workloads. The company plans to commence manufacturing FDX Fusion technology in 2028 at its advanced facility in Dresden, Germany, reinforcing the site’s role as a strategic European hub for differentiated semiconductor technologies.
The first generation of FDX Fusion technology is expected to deliver seven nanometer class digital performance and is being developed from the ground up as the next major extension of GF’s FDX ™ FD-SOI roadmap. By combining advanced substrate engineering, front-end transistor innovation and back-end interconnect and integration capabilities with exceptional RF performance up to 0.5 THz ft/fmax, analog and mixed-signal features, low-leakage operation, in-memory computing capabilities, embedded non-volatile memory and dense logic, FDX Fusion is expected to deliver more than 2x density improvement over first-generation FDX technology. This approach aims to provide customers with a comprehensive, intelligent platform for edge and Physical AI applications while reducing system complexity, latency and power consumption.
“Physical AI is creating a new class of semiconductor requirements as intelligence moves beyond the cloud and into systems and devices that can process data in real time and interact seamlessly with the physical environment,” said Ed Kaste, senior vice president of GF’s CMOS business. “The FDX Fusion platform extends GF’s FD-SOI roadmap with innovations across the substrate, transistor and interconnect stack, delivering a platform purpose-built for power-efficient Physical AI applications. Combined with our software-to-silicon capabilities and our expanding, resilient manufacturing footprint in Europe, FDX Fusion will position GF as the technology partner of choice to accelerate the scaling of Physical AI.”
The new platform builds on the company’s longstanding leadership in FD-SOI technology and power-efficient semiconductor design for secure, connected devices, with billions of chips in use today across a broad range of applications including automotive radars and sensors, wireless microcontrollers, display drivers and front-end modules for SATCOM and 5G devices.
FDX Fusion is expected to address a broad range of Physical AI systems and applications across the automotive, consumer and industrial markets, including edge inference, robotics, industrial automation, autonomous systems, sensor-fusion architectures and intelligent connected devices. GF is engaged with several customers on early development and evaluation for FDX Fusion, using real application requirements to inform product design and accelerate the technology’s progress from platform definition to production readiness.
To accelerate time-to-market for FDX Fusion designs, customers can leverage GF’s broad design enablement ecosystem, including its advanced MIPS and ARC portfolio with workload-driven processor IP, RISC-V instruction set architecture (ISA) and application-specific processor design capabilities optimized for Physical AI. These resources will complement the FDX Fusion platform with scalable, standards-based solutions across the full Physical AI signal chain and enable GF to support customers through every step of the design cycle, from compute architecture development to high-volume silicon production.
Initial manufacturing for FDX Fusion technology is planned for GF’s Dresden facility, where ongoing expansion efforts supported under the framework of the European Chips Act are increasing capacity for differentiated semiconductor solutions critical to security and defense, industrial competitiveness, supply chain resilience and European technological sovereignty. Through its expansion and strategic technology roadmap, GF aims to accelerate Europe’s leadership in developing and manufacturing the technologies underpinning AI-enabled industrial systems, secure connectivity and next-generation intelligent systems.
Demonstrator silicon for FDX Fusion technology is targeted for early customer evaluation in early 2027, with an initial process design kit (PDK) release planned for mid-2027. The platform will also include optimized process flow and cost structures for rapid prototyping and faster time-to-market.
Future automotive applications will require increasingly integrated and energy-efficient semiconductor solutions that combine AI processing, sensing, real-time control and secure connectivity. articles.title_orig: From the school store to the real world: Princeton students put business skills to work
articles.title_zh: From the school store to the real world: Princeton students put business skills to work
articles.content_orig:
PRINCETON, W.Va. (WCHS) — At Princeton Senior High School, business class is about a lot more than taking notes and studying from a textbook.
Students are putting their skills to work through the school store, marketing campaigns, athletics promotions and other hands-on projects designed to prepare them for life after graduation.
The Den, Princeton’s school store, is run by students and gives them a chance to experience what it is like to work in a real business.
“Actually we run this store in here. We sell a lot of merch, Tiger gear,” Senior Daethon Thomas said.
Students help sell Tiger gear, snacks and drinks while gaining experience with money management, customer service, communication and teamwork.
“I like to do hands-on stuff, so a lot of kids, I would say, they prefer to do that too. And this helps a lot with communication,” Thomas said.
The school store is just one part of Princeton’s business department.
Business teacher Chelsea Murphy said students can complete four business courses as part of the program. Along the way, they build a career portfolio they can use for college applications, job interviews and scholarships.
“It consists of a cover letter, resume, letters of recommendation and certifications that they've earned while they've been in our program,” Murphy said.
Students also get the chance to put their creative skills to work.
Recently, business students created a 30-day marketing campaign for homecoming. Their work included flyers, social media posts, videos and a homecoming logo that has been used throughout the school.
“It’s really fun because we get to design things. It’s not just taking notes and letting our teacher run it. It’s more student centered,” junior Brielle Coburn said.
The program serves more than 150 juniors and seniors each year, giving students plenty of opportunities to build skills they can carry with them after high school.
Junior Brystal Winfrey said the lessons extend well beyond the classroom.
“I think the business teachers are really good at making sure we know how to manage our money, finances, marketing. So I think those things would really transfer into the future,” junior Brystal Winfrey said.
For Coburn, the creative skills she has learned in business class could even help her in her future career as an elementary teacher.
“I’m going to be an elementary teacher, so in elementary it’s super important to have things that are colorful and eye catching. So Miss Murphy has taught me a lot about how I can teach from different things,” Coburn said.
Murphy said that is exactly the goal of the program: giving students tangible skills they can use wherever life takes them.
“Because business is life, right? So we can use our standards and we develop our lessons to show students that what we’re doing here is what you can do when you walk out of these doors,” Murphy said.
From running a school store to creating a homecoming campaign, Princeton students are getting a taste of the business world before they even graduate.
They are not just learning how to run a business. They are learning how to run with their future.

articles.title_orig: UNAIDS at the World Health Summit 2026
articles.title_zh: UNAIDS at the World Health Summit 2026
articles.content_orig:
This year’s World Health Summit will be held in Berlin, Germany from 11 to 13 October under the theme: From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health. At the Summit UNAIDS will share its knowledge and expertise in the future of the HIV response, global health financing, pandemic preparedness and inequalities that are preventing progress. The World Health Summit 2026 takes place at a critical moment. In June, countries adopted a new Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS, reaffirming the goal to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. The focus now must shift from political commitment to implementation. This year has seen a sequence of major milestones, including the High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS, AIDS 2026 and UNGA81. Together, these events and commitments have helped draw from the AIDS response to further debates on equitable financing, health sovereignty, pandemic preparedness, resilience and the future of multilateral cooperation. It also coincides with a pivotal moment for the future of the UNAIDS and its transformation. UNAIDS objectives at the World Health Summit:
Sunday 11 October 9:00-10:30 Global health architecture reform: From recommendations to action at the regional and country levels This session focuses on what reform looks like from the regional and country level. The discussion will explore "what's actually changing" and "what's next". The session draws on experiences from countries, regional institutions, funders, and global actors to examine whether a more regionalised approach can make global health cooperation more responsive, coherent, and accountable. 11:00-12.30 Advancing equitable, person-centred HIV prevention and care in Europe This side event, co-organized by the International AIDS Society (IAS) and AIDS action Europe, will highlight how person-centred, community-led HIV prevention and care informed by lived experience can reshape and redefine service delivery and related policies. It will reinforce why community-led systems must be recognized and resourced as integral to public health delivery. At a time of shifting global financing priorities and growing pressure on health systems, the event will provide a platform for exchange on enabling policies and examples of person-centred HIV programming to expand access to HIV testing, prevention, care and related services for people living with HIV and populations vulnerable to HIV acquisition. Monday 12 October 11:00-12:00 Long-acting innovation, lasting impact: Advancing the global HIV response The discussion will feature Mark Dybul, former Executive Director of the Global Fund and former U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator leading PEPFAR, who will share an exclusive preview of Rockefeller-funded economic modelling from Imperial College London and Georgetown University examining the potential impact of accelerating the rollout of long-acting PrEP for populations at higher risk of acquiring HIV across high-, middle- and low-income settings. The event will also explore barriers to countries and at-risk populations accessing long-acting HIV prevention and treatment options, with a particular focus on regulatory, financing and supply chain challenges, with a deep dive into the unique barriers faced by middle-income countries and regions. 14:00-15:30 G7 and G20: Fit for future global health challenges? The G7 and G20 have played a pivotal role in shaping global health agendas. Through their convening power, they have translated shared priorities into coordinated responses, have mobilized resources and fostered tangible political action. This session will examine where both fora stand today, how they interact with another, and whether the G7 and G20 remain fit-for-purpose to advance global health priorities: Should they be adapted to continue driving effective global health action in an increasingly multipolar world? 14:00-15:30 RoundTable discussion - Resilience in the HIV response: From innovation to impact Aligning with this year’s Summit theme of resilience and innovation, this special session will be a roundtable discussion with a facilitated conversation between legislators and experts, focused on policy leadership in the HIV response. Discussions will cover the latest innovations in the HIV response and the role of legislators in driving implementation; how to build resilience into public health systems; sustainable financing; and the necessary political priorities to ensure the HIV response delivers equitable public health outcomes for key populations. 18.00-19.30 World Health Summit signature event: “From crisis to resilience: Innovating for health” How can global health move from a crisis response to lasting resilience and turn shared ambition into concrete action? The World Health Summit 2026 Signature Event will bring together global leaders, multilateral institutions, youth voices and partners in philanthropy and innovation to explore the political choices, institutional changes, and innovations needed to deliver better health for all.
Tuesday 13 October 09:00-10:30 Safeguarding the global HIV response in a changing multilateral environment This workshop brings together donors, policymakers, civil society and UN system representatives. Looking ahead, the session will consider what lessons the UNAIDS experience may offer for wider multilateral reform efforts, such as the UN80 reform process, particularly how institutions can work in a more efficient and coordinated manner, while increasing specialization, legitimacy, accountability and responsiveness including to communities and CSOs.
