articles.title_orig: ‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
articles.title_zh: ‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
articles.content_orig:
The United States government has moved to exclude some of the world’s top tech companies from a programme that allows them to sponsor skilled foreign workers for permanent residency.
Vice President JD Vance said the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of US workers.
It comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration continues efforts to clamp down on immigration – both legal and undocumented – and make it harder for immigrants to get residency or citizenship.
But the latest move also potentially impacts thousands of foreign workers, many of whom have spent years waiting for a backlog in applications to clear.
Here’s what to know about the latest policy:
The suspension concerns the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, which enables a US-based employer to sponsor a foreign worker’s green card — as the permanent residency is commonly known. To qualify, the employer is supposed to demonstrate that there are insufficient US workers for a needed job role and that bringing a foreign worker will not impact the pay or conditions of US workers in the industry.
PERM is a key step in the green card process for many skilled foreign workers. Major tech companies often hire workers on temporary visas, such as the H-1B, before they transition to permanent residency through the PERM process.
Vance on Thursday accused major companies of fraudulently using the current visa regime to displace US employees and bring in lower-paid foreign workers who amount to “indentured servants”.
“The programme has become rife with fraud,” said Vance at a White House news conference. He claimed that many workers who start off on temporary H-1B visas and later apply for permanent residency under the PERM programme are “being mistreated by their employers” and “used to undercut the wages of American workers”.
“You’ve got to hire great American workers,” the US vice president said. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling used similar language, saying the US would “shut down the pipeline of systemic fraud that has flooded our country”.
“The fraud doesn’t end with getting the job,” said Sonderling. “That job becomes a pathway for foreign workers and their families to stay in America permanently and eventually (become) US citizens.”
“And who pays for it all? The American worker,” he said.
Vance singled out Microsoft as a major offender and said it would be suspended from the PERM programme.
Other companies whose PERM applications will no longer be processed include US software firm Adobe and some of the world’s top IT firms, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Of these, Capgemini is French, Microsoft and Adobe are American, and the rest — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL — are all Indian.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” said Sonderling.
Vance said the suspensions would continue “as long as it needs to”.
Other companies that rely heavily on H-1B visas such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet’s Google will not be affected.
Critics of the H-1B visa and PERM green card process argue that some employers use the system not to fill legitimate skills shortages, but to reduce labour costs, gain leverage over workers and make it harder for US employees to compete for jobs. They say companies do this by hiring foreign workers at lower wages and manipulating recruitment conditions to keep out qualified US workers.
Vance said Microsoft last year let go 6,000 US workers, while also securing 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vance.
Sonderling said companies being suspended from PERM had received more than 230,000 H-1B visas and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications since 2009.
“That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.
The H1-B visa system has also emerged as a lightning rod for many of the most vocal backers of Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, some of whom have married criticism of the programme with anti-immigrant stereotypes  — particularly against Indians — to demand that the scheme be scrapped.
Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented new hires replacing US workers. In a statement, the company said that 80 percent of the roughly 6,000 H1-B visa applications it issued last year were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees”, not for new employees, and that the other filings were for “individuals already legally in the United States”.
The company also said that it only files applications for people who “meet the rigorous standards of this visa category” and that such employees are paid equally to any others who do similar work.
The suspension could make it harder for foreign workers in the tech industry to obtain permanent residency in the US. Many of those affected are likely to be Indian nationals, who account for a large share of the country’s skilled foreign workforce in the technology sector.
Each year, there are only 85,000 slots for new H-1B visas (not including filings for renewals), but hundreds of thousands of applications. Many H-1B visa holders work in technology-related jobs: 62 percent of the beneficiaries in the 2025 fiscal year worked in computer-related occupations.
Indian nationals account for roughly 70 percent of existing H-1B visa holders.
The Trump administration has already tried to crack down on the H1-B scheme, and in August proposed a new $103,000 fee for H1-B applications, after an earlier pitch for a similar fee was struck down by a federal court. The fee, the government argues, would help provide revenue that could be used to service the vast US immigration system, while reducing the incentive for companies to attempt to misuse H1-B visas.
But the new move to restrict the pathway to a green card for foreign workers already in the US, legally, could impact not just those who might have dreamed of working or living in the US — but thousands already in the country.
The US typically issues around 140,000 employment-based green cards every year. But it also has a strict country-based cap — applicants from any one country cannot receive more than seven percent of green cards issued in a year.
Yet, because the employment-based green card application system is largely used to convert many H1-B visa holders into permanent residents, applicants for permanent residency are disproportionately Indian.
The result: Nearly one million Indians legally in the US on work visas are currently stuck in the employment-based green card backlog. They represent 79 percent of the total green card backlog of around 1.25 million people.
Even before the latest move, Indian green card applicants in certain employment categories would have needed to wait for decades, according to a 2025 analysis for the Congressional Research Service.
Sonderling’s statement that the US will no longer process “any pending permanent labour certification applications” from the blacklisted companies has raised fears that tens of thousands of foreign workers in the country legally — most of them Indian — who have waited for years might suddenly no longer be eligible. For others, the wait could get even longer.
Yes. India’s Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement saying the US’s suspension does not “advance the shared ambitions of both countries”.
The ministry said that “talent mobility adds value” to both the Indian and US economies, including providing US companies “with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation”.

NEW YORK (AP) — Lower oil prices are helping to propel the U.S. stock market to the finish of a record-setting week, but financial markets remain indecisive. The S&P 500 rose 0.3% early Friday and clawed back some of its two straight days of losses since setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 82 points, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.6%. The moves were tentative as oil prices continue to yo-yo because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. Treasury yields flipped up and down in the bond market.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
U.S. futures are climbing and as oil prices retreated from their recent gains after President Donald Trump said “productive discussions” are happening with Iran.
Futures for the S&P 500 gained 0.4% on Friday, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.1%. Nasdaq futures rose 0.7%.
Trump said in a social media post on Thursday that his team has been “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.” He also indicated that he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States.
Brent crude oil declined 1.2% on Friday to $103.01 a barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude oil fell 0.9% to $90.69 a barrel.
The drop in oil prices comes after stocks felt pressure on Thursday from a 4.1% rise in the price for a barrel of Brent, the international standard, to more than $104. It’s been pinballing between $96 and nearly $110 over the last month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
In the bond market, yields have been trading at their highest levels in years or even decades, threatening to slow the economy.
The 10-year Treasury yield initially rose to 5.35% on Thursday before falling back to 5.23%. It edged up slightly to 5.25% on Friday.
The yield's fluctuations came after the U.S. government said that it sold $22 billion in 30-year Treasury bonds at an auction with a high yield of less than 5.62%. That helped bring the 30-year Treasury yield down to 5.60% from 5.73% on Thursday, which is a notable move for the bond market. It was at 5.62% on Friday.
High debt loads have loomed over the market as the U.S. federal deficit climbed to nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended on Sept. 30.
Investors are also continuing to keep an eye on the latest earnings reports. On Friday shares of Delta Air Lines dropped more than 4% before the market open after the airline reported a quarterly profit that missed estimates. Delta also trimmed its full-year estimate for earnings per share, citing a $6 billion increase in fuel costs.
Several of the country’s biggest banks release quarterly results next week.
Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30% in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to data provider FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third consecutive quarter of growth that exceeds 25%.
In Europe, the German DAX climbed 1% to 25,044.82, while the CAC 40 in Paris gained 0.6% to 7,775.44. Britain's FTSE 100 rose 0.9% to 10,538.88. Asian markets were mixed. Markets were closed in South Korea and Taiwan.
China is due to release its latest economic growth figures next week.
In other dealings, the U.S. dollar rose to 158.29 Japanese yen from 157.89 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1210, edging lower from $1.1211.

articles.title_orig: Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
articles.title_zh: Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
articles.content_orig:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.
We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?
Something is breaking in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
This story was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed. Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, professor Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian reported in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem. The new study, published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology , indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird — which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek — may need to be classified as an endangered species.
Zavodovski Island had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic Peninsula to 5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity Peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4°C, about 20°C above normal for the time of year — a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy.”
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30 percent — though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “ Penguin Pompeii hypothesis ” of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

The net worth of the richest person in the world is nearly three times that of the billionaire with the second-largest fortune.
While the world's wealthiest people often swap places on the rich list, one person has held the top spot since 2025: Tesla CEO and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.
In total, the five richest people in the world have a combined net worth of $2.2 trillion, according to Bloomberg's Billionaire Index . Using the same index, we explore their wealth in detail below.
As the wealthiest bunch are all men, we take a look at the richest woman in the world in a separate guide.
Elon Musk is the richest person in the world, with a staggering $987 billion to his name.
The South African entrepreneur has added over $500 billion to his net worth in the past year, thanks to buzz around the SpaceX initial public offering (IPO) .
Musk first crossed the trillion-dollar mark in June after SpaceX went public, reaching an estimated fortune of $1.45 trillion, though he has since lost that status.
However, he is still richer than the three billionaires right below him on the rich list combined.
Musk owns around 11% of Tesla and roughly 50% of SpaceX.
Jeff Bezos has a net worth of $365 billion. The billionaire is most famous for founding Amazon in 1994, which started when Bezos saw a gap in the market for e-commerce and began to sell books online, working out of his garage. Now, the empire has a market capitalisation of $2.7 trillion.
Bezos owns The Washington Post , one of the largest newspapers in the United States. He also has a stake in Blue Origin, a space exploration company he founded in 2000. Blue Origin's latest funding round has added billions to his fortune, making him the second-richest person in the world.
Bezos is increasingly looking to dominate the world of film and fashion. He was the lead sponsor and honorary co-chair of the 2026 Met Gala and donated $10 million, making it the largest individual financial commitment in the event's history.
Last year, Amazon took creative control of the James Bond franchise. Back in 2021, it acquired MGM Studios, a historic American production company, for $8.45 billion. Some of MGM's most popular films include The Wizard of Oz , Gone with the Wind and 2001: A Space Odyssey .
Larry Page's net worth currently stands at $298 billion. He founded Google in 1998 with Sergey Brin, who is also on the rich list.
A majority of Page's wealth comes from his stake in Google, which rebranded as Alphabet in 2015, grouping all its divisions – including Gmail, Android and YouTube – under one umbrella.
Page stepped down as CEO of Alphabet in 2019, but he remains a board member and a controlling shareholder of the company.
Sergey Brin, co-founder of Alphabet, has a net worth of $277 billion, not far behind that of fellow co-founder Larry Page.
The American businessman was the president of Alphabet until 2019, and has since remained a board member and a controlling shareholder.
Brin has been donating millions of dollars worth of his shares in Alphabet to fund research on Parkinson's disease. He was recently awarded the National Medal of Science by US president Donald Trump at the Institute of Peace in Washington.
Michael Dell is a new entrant to this list, with a net worth of $265 billion. He is the founder and CEO of Dell Technologies and owns 40% of the company.
It was founded in 1984 when Dell was studying at the University of Texas, and initially operated out of his university dorm room, where he sold personal computers directly to customers.
The business was originally called PC's Limited, and it went public in 1988. In 1992, Michael Dell became the youngest CEO in Fortune's list of the top 500 corporations. Dell was formed in 2016 through a $60 billion merger with EMC.
Since 2025, Michael Dell has added more than $100 billion to his wealth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index . Shares in the company have risen by more than 300% since the start of the year, and it has also helped Dell shoot past Meta's Mark Zuckerberg on the rich list.

articles.title_orig: Labour Holds Off Green Party in Election for Starmer’s Former London Seat
articles.title_zh: Labour Holds Off Green Party in Election for Starmer’s Former London Seat
articles.content_orig:
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.
The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.
Lichtenstein's comments come after former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.
Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that.
The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year .
Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.
In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with – it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee."
Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.
The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom".
She later posted on X to clarify she was "not calling on Zack to step down" and she welcomed that Polanski had "indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion".
"Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward," she said.
Polanski defended his absence from the controversial motion vote in Brighton, saying he was busy campaigning in the North London constituency.
Asked if he would resign, he said: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."
He added:  "Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."
Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.
However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".
Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.
On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist.
"I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."
Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."
In private, plenty of longstanding Green figures remain frustrated and accuse Polanski of being "missing in action" over the motion.
They say the result is an untenable situation where he leads a party whose policy on the Middle East he disagrees with.
"He is in danger of losing the confidence of both wings," one critic pointed out, referring to how some supporters of the motion have now been left irritated too by Polanski's refusal to publicly back them.
But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.
Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit.
"I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now around the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.
Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".
The party's next scheduled leadership ballot takes place in summer 2027 - and Bartley said he thinks Polanski will face a challenger.
Sian Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said on Friday she was ready to work with colleagues "to restore trust in our processes and our party, fix the serious flaws in the motion that was passed" and build more inclusive policies.
The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.
Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons with her party's previous antisemitism scandal , telling the BBC she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.
Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.

articles.title_orig: Man shot by ICE agent in New York City's Marble Hill, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Man shot by ICE agent in New York City's Marble Hill, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
A man was hospitalized after being shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in New York City's Marble Hill neighborhood on Thursday, according to the Department of Homeland Security and New York City officials.
The shooting occurred at about 4 p.m. local time near West 225th Street and Marble Hill Avenue.
In a press conference Thursday night , NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said ICE agents tried to arrest a man in a car with a 5-year-old boy in the backseat. One ICE agent fired seven rounds at the car, striking the 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the neck, Tisch said.
Officials said he was taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. The child was not injured and is in the care of a family member, Tisch said.
The NYPD was not involved in the shooting, the department said.
DHS, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement that officers were conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest a man from the Dominican Republic who they allege was living in the United States illegally.
DHS alleged that the man had associations to the Trinitarios gang. Tisch said he has two prior arrests. In 2023, he was arrested on a robbery charge and later pleaded guilty to fourth-degree larceny. He was also arrested in 2025 on a charge of criminal sale of a controlled substance, a case that remains pending.
Tisch said NYPD cameras captured a vehicle backing into a parking spot in front of a fire hydrant. She says video shows one plainclothes federal law enforcement officer approaching the driver's side window with his gun drawn and a second plainclothes officer approaching the vehicle by the driver's side headlight. According Tisch, the vehicle then moves forward out of view of the camera.
An ICE officer discharged his weapon during the incident, injuring the man, DHS said.
"ICE officers immediately rendered aid," DHS said. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital. The FBI and HSI are on the scene. The incident remains under investigation. More information will be shared as it becomes available."
Tisch said NYPD officers who were in the area responded to the scene after hearing reports of shots fired.
"When they arrived, they encountered several men in various forms of attire, including some in construction-style vests, face masks and at least one carrying a long gun," she said.
Tisch said Belgal was handcuffed and seated on the ground. According to Tisch, NYPD officers placed him into an NYPD vehicle, rendered aid and transported him to the hospital.
Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York told CBS News in an interview Thursday night that the 5-year-old child was the son of Belgal. Espaillat told CBS News that he met with the 5-year-old boy and his mother at the hospital, where Belgal received treatment.
Espaillat disclosed Belgal was under guard by ICE agents outside his hospital room, and Espaillat was not allowed to see him.
Late Thursday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said ICE "put the man in an unmarked vehicle and whisked him away."
Mamdani said he spent two hours on the phone with President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night to negotiate for the release of Belgal, but those negotiations were unsuccessful.
Federal agencies have taken over the investigation, Tisch said.
The NYPD said five people were taken into custody during protests that broke out over the shooting.
Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called for a "full and independent investigation" of the incident and the release of all body camera video that captured it. She also said in a statement Thursday night that, "The Target Corporation must stop offering their Bronx properties as private staging sites for ICE, in compliance with requests from New York officials. Target opening up large, active retail parking lots for paramilitary activity is unacceptable and places the entire community at risk."
CBS News has reached out to Target for comment.
There have been at least 30 shootings involving DHS officers during the second Trump administration, according to a CBS News analysis, some of which have turned deadly.
Camilo  Montoya-Galvez contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: A Volkswagen bestseller goes electric: world premiere of the new ID. Tiguan
articles.title_zh: A Volkswagen bestseller goes electric: world premiere of the new ID. Tiguan
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen presents the new ID. Tiguan, one of the brand’s most important electric models for the years ahead. The new all-round SUV in the high-volume mid-size class succeeds the ID.4 and ID.5 models. The ID. Tiguan’s hallmark feature is its completely redesigned exterior, which gives it the appearance of a vehicle from the next class up. And this impression continues seamlessly into the strikingly high-quality interior: the materials used have resulted in a huge leap forwards in terms of quality, complemented by the newly developed, intuitive cockpit landscape. For the first time, the new SUV will be available with a co-driver display . The electrically powered ID. Tiguan will be launched as early as the beginning of 2027 – in parallel to the current Tiguan with petrol, diesel and hybrid drives.
Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the Volkswagen brand, Head of the Brand Group Core and member of the Group Board of Management: “The Tiguan is our  best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most  successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success  stories together. A pure, confident design with the presence of a  vehicle from the next class up, intuitive operation and, thanks to MEB+,  a range of up to 600 kilometres : a new  benchmark for our electric SUVs made in Germany. Together with the  Tiguan from Wolfsburg, the ID. Tiguan from Emden is part of one of the  strongest SUV duos in Europe.”
Range of up to 600 km and a maximum towing capacity of 2,000 kg. Volkswagen will offer the ID. Tiguan in three performance levels:
Depending on the power and battery size, the WLTP ranges will reach up to 600 km . At the same time, the model impresses with its high suitability for everyday use: the towing capacity is up to 1,800 kg with the 58 kWh battery, and up to 2,000 kg with the 77 kWh battery. In addition, there is a frunk with 32 litres of stowage space and a luggage compartment volume of up to 534 litres. Functional, comfortable or sporty: the ID. Tiguan will be available in the four equipment versions Trend, Life, Style and R-Line.
Progress visible everywhere. Volkswagen has specifically incorporated customer requests into the development of the new ID. Tiguan, implementing countless enhancements and advanced technologies. Taking the cockpit landscape as an example, highlights include a co-driver display (12-inch, 30.5-cm diagonal), the first time a feature like this has appeared in a European Volkswagen. The 10-inch driver display (Digital Cockpit, 25.4-cm diagonal) and the central 15-inch infotainment display (38.1-cm diagonal) are also new. Together with the co-driver display, this results in a continuous display landscape that opens up a new world, especially for the front passenger – one where they can immerse themselves in their own world of infotainment, information, and gaming without distracting the driver. This is because the display is not visible to the driver, as with a laptop privacy screen (privacy mode). In privacy mode, the front passenger can listen to the sound on their paired Bluetooth headphones.
The ID. Tiguan embodies a new design language. One of Volkswagen’s core values is a superior and timeless design. And this is embodied in every way by the new ID. Tiguan. The Pure Positive design language has a major influence on the exterior design of the ID. Tiguan: the softer crossover design of the predecessors has given way to a powerful SUV design with a strong visual presence. Precise lines and tightly sculpted surfaces lend it additional stability and quality. As a result, the new model looks like a vehicle from the premium segment. In addition, Volkswagen is returning to classic pull-style door handles with the ID. Tiguan.
On a premium level. The interior also boasts a clear, high-quality design, intuitive controls, a  premium feel and an atmosphere that is welcoming in every respect. This  feeling is reinforced by elegant lighting effects. The interplay of  design, materials and a stylish colour scheme creates an atmosphere  reminiscent of the next segment above.
Intuitive operation. Volkswagen has implemented a clear operating logic throughout the ID. Tiguan. Important functions can therefore be accessed using physical buttons again and have been incorporated into the interior where you would intuitively expect to find them. The air conditioning system is a prime example of this: the basic functions are now controlled via a button bar in the centre console. The door openers in the interior are another example: they are ergonomically optimised to sit perfectly in the hand. In this area on the driver’s side, the in-door control panel for the four power windows has also been redesigned. A further example is the process for adjusting the audio volume and changing the station/track, which is performed primarily using an intuitively accessible controller in the centre console. Positioned at the front: two inductive charging points compliant with the Qi2 standard; integrated magnetic rings position and secure compatible smartphones precisely on the charging points. Another new feature is the multifunction steering wheel with physical buttons instead of touch controls.
New ‘Retro’ displays. In spite of all the focus on functionality, there is also an element of fun as demonstrated by the ‘Retro’ displays. These are a brand-new development for the ID. Tiguan. If the driver activates the ‘Retro’ display using the ‘View’ button on the multifunction steering wheel, the iconic blue-red instruments from a Golf IV appear in the Digital Cockpit. In this case, there is a classic speedometer on the left and a stylised rev counter on the right. It does not display engine speeds but the energy flow in the drive as a power display. The corresponding ‘Retro’ view in the central infotainment screen can also be personalised for the first time. Here, the driver can choose from six different Volkswagen models, which are displayed in a virtual garage: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg and Beetle.
Innovative technologies, optional equipment. Modern assistance, driving and comfort systems are available for the new ID.   Tiguan. These include features such as the standard-equipment one-pedal   driving (strong deceleration using the accelerator pedal alone), the  new  Connected Travel Assist , which, among  other  things, enables assisted lane changing on motorways and automatically stops  the  ID. Tiguan at red traffic lights .
In addition, comfort features  such as  electrically adjustable front seats with  massage, memory and ventilation functions as well as  a high-end sound  system from Harman Kardon  with an output of 480  watts and a panoramic sunroof will be part of  the optional equipment range.
Well thought-out down to the last detail. A practical and flexible feature is the Digital Key . This enables the vehicle to be unlocked, locked and  started using a compatible smartphone. The Digital Key can also be  transferred to family members, friends or colleagues – using the  Volkswagen app, it can be shared easily by means of text message,  messenger services or email. Another clever and practical solution is  the PowerSocket for Vehicle-to-Load. This  adapter is simply plugged into the charging socket of the ID. Tiguan and  can be used to power all kinds of electrical devices – from electric  grills to e-bikes.
Pre-sales for the ID. Tiguan start in Germany  and many other European countries on 13 October at prices from 42,695  euros .

articles.title_orig: Steering through danger: the WFP drivers keeping Ukrainians fed
articles.title_zh: Steering through danger: the WFP drivers keeping Ukrainians fed
articles.content_orig:
The mission started like any other. Driver Vasyl was behind the wheel of a World Food Programme (WFP) truck – part of a humanitarian convoy heading to Bilozerka, a small town in southern Ukraine ’s Kherson Region, roughly 10 kilometres from the frontline of a war now in its fifth year.
The four-truck convoy carried humanitarian assistance including medicine, hygiene and shelter items for the 1,400 residents remaining in the town – formerly home to 9,000. As the line of vehicles neared the entrance of Bilozerka, a small bomb-laden drone detonated on the road.
Then another drone struck even closer.
“We jumped into the armoured car and quickly drove away,” Vasyl recounts (last names in this story are being withheld protectively). As they escaped, members of the convoy heard his truck getting hit multiple times. By the time it was safe to go back, the vehicle was completely engulfed in flames.
If I had been inside, I don't think I would have survived.” WFP driver Vasyl.
The drones hit the cab where Vasyl had been sitting minutes earlier. “If I had been inside, I don't think I would have survived,” he says.
No one in the convoy was hurt. But the convoy’s humanitarian supplies had all gone up in smoke.
Such incidents are becoming increasingly common for humanitarian drivers in Ukraine. They are on the road every day to bring food and other lifesaving assistance to communities living closest to the frontline – where shops are often closed, and prices are high.
That makes WFP’s support — reaching more than 600,000 Ukrainians in frontline areas with food and cash each month — all the more important. Tapping our fleet of WFP trucks and our logistics expertise , our weekly convoys also carry not only food but essential humanitarian supplies such as health and shelter items from other United Nations agencies and nongovernmental groups.
But a surge in drone attacks over the last year has drastically complicated movements and deliveries, with trucks, passenger vehicles and gas stations frequently targeted. Anti-drone nets, which authorities have erected over hundreds of kilometres of the main axes crossing frontline regions, only partially reduce the threat.
Since 2023, WFP’s own tracking has recorded a total of 120 security incidents affecting WFP operations and our cooperating partners. So far this year, 43 incidents have been recorded – more than triple the total recorded in all of 2023.
“It was emotionally hard,” Vasyl recalls of the explosion he survived. “The realization that my children could have been left without a father came later. That's probably the hardest part.
“Before this incident, we were careful,” he adds. “Now we're three times more careful.”
Born in a small town in western Ukraine ’s Rivne Region, Vasyl has been behind the wheel for twenty years, steering vans and buses long before the war. Even today, on the quieter drives along Ukraine’s sunflower fields, he sometimes stops to buy pies and fresh vegetables from roadside sellers to carry home to his wife and two daughters.
His wife worries each time he leaves on mission. He rarely shares the full details to spare her the distress. His daughters, though, are well aware of the risks and have always supported his decision to keep going.
Andrii has been working in the humanitarian field since 2012. In fourteen years on the road, he has never experienced anything like this year, when he survived two convoy attacks.
The first attack came this past March in the Donetsk Region, within 20 kilometres of the frontline. Andrii was driving the tail vehicle when a drone hit the truck ahead of him.
“I thought it was just a branch falling. Then suddenly the truck caught on fire,” he recalls. “Following protocol, I quickly backed up my vehicle.”
His team pulled the injured driver from the truck’s cab and rushed him to the nearest hospital, where he underwent surgery. Everyone survived.
“You don't feel anything in the moment,” Andrii says. “You're just doing your job. It's scary before and after. During, you just do what needs to be done. Afterward, when you start processing what happened, that's when the fear comes.”
“Our job is to help people stay alive. So we keep going." – WFP driver Andrii
The second strike came in July: 20 minutes from the frontline in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk Region, as Andrii’s convoy was on its way back from delivering assistance.
“Our armoured vehicle was hit, and the whole car jumped up,” Andrii says. “But thankfully everyone was safe. The cab was still usable, so we continued our way back to Dnipro city.”
He describes a vigilance that never fully switches off. “We always look around when we drive. Of course it's frightening, it's always frightening,” he says, ”because these hits come like lightning. You never know when they will start or when they will stop.”
After the first strike, the image stayed with him: flashbacks surfacing at night. The memory of a truck tearing apart, replaying at unexpected moments. “It gets harder and harder to keep driving,” he admits.
But his commitment hasn't changed.
“Our job is to help people stay alive,” Andrii says. “So we keep going. For us the goal of any mission stays the same: to return safely.”
For people waiting for these frontline deliveries, the WFP food boxes are a lifeline. Residents near these battle zones describe a daily struggle to access basic necessities in places where shops have shuttered and few opportunities exist to earn an income.
Many remaining are elderly or live with disabilities. Even reaching shops in nearby areas can be dangerous.
“It's not easy for us to get to the shops because drones are constantly flying,” says Tetiana, who lives in a frontline village in southern Kherson.
But for another WFP driver, Oleksandr, the frontline evokes another sentiment.
“Work missions bring me home, even if it's only for an hour. I know every road, every turn,” he says. "It feels like going back home.”
“It's a heavy nostalgia - knowing your homeland is right there, and that you can't go.” WFP driver Oleksandr of his hometown in the occupied Donetsk Region.
His hometown lies just a few kilometres from the routes he now drives for work, close enough that he can almost see it. It’s just two fields away, he says, but still completely unreachable: on the other side of the frontline in occupied Donetsk.
“It's a heavy nostalgia,” he says. “Knowing your homeland is right there, and that you can't go.”
The land makes itself known as soon as you get near, he says, the particular odor of Donbas: the smoky metallic smell of terikony —large, coneshaped hills of mining by-products, a symbol of the Donbas landscape, mixed with scorched steppe grass and the sweetness of ripening summer orchards. It is a heavy agrarian region, thick with the odor of a place that has always lived off its soil.
“Even the air pressure feels different there,” he says. “You just know you're home.”
Despite the risks, Oleksandr, Andrii and Vasyl continue to help bring food and humanitarian assistance every week to hundreds of thousands of their fellow Ukrainians still living in frontline areas. Yet, since the beginning of the year, WFP has lost access to 354 settlements due to worsening security, leaving more than 15,000 people cut off from vital humanitarian support.
WFP’s Logistics Cluster, which coordinates weekly humanitarian convoys to frontline areas of Ukraine, is generously funded by the European Union.

articles.title_zh: SpaceX brings four astronauts home after 8 months in space, and the return was flawless
articles.content_orig:
Four Crew-12 members are back on Earth after 237 days at the International Space Station. SpaceX’s Crew Dragon Freedom splashed down in the Pacific Ocean about 50 miles west of Los Angeles at 11:34 a.m. ET on Thursday.
NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev landed one day after undocking from the station’s Harmony module at 8:05 a.m. ET on Wednesday. NASA confirmed the splashdown minutes later. SpaceX had flagged the 27.5 hour trip home on X while Dragon was still firing its departure burns away from the station.
The descent ran on schedule when Freedom started a nine minute deorbit burn at 10:46 a.m. ET, then hit the thicker atmosphere about 36 minutes later at nearly five miles per second. Chutes deployed at around 18,000 feet, and four main parachutes brought the capsule down to roughly 15 mph at splashdown.
SpaceX fast boats secured Dragon before the recovery ship Shannon hoisted it onto the deck with the crew still inside. Flight surgeons on board ran initial medical checks. All four crew members will be flown ashore by helicopter and then head to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston for rehabilitation.

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 8, 2026
Crew-12 launched on February 13 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral, a flight that also marked the first Falcon 9 booster landing at SpaceX’s new LZ-40 pad. Over the mission, the crew completed 3,792 orbits, covered nearly 101 million miles, and carried out four spacewalks to maintain and upgrade the station.
Meir now has 440 cumulative days in space, which places her in NASA’s top 10. This was the first spaceflight for Hathaway and for Adenot, a French Air Force colonel and former helicopter pilot. Fedyaev, who spent 186 days in orbit on Crew-6 in 2023, has now flown two long duration Dragon missions.
The return closes out a busy stretch of Dragon traffic. Crew-13 arrived on October 1 aboard Crew Dragon Grace , which docked just 7 hours and 55 minutes after liftoff , the fastest launch to docking of any U.S. spacecraft in ISS history. Commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov remain aboard alongside the three person Soyuz MS-29 crew.
With Crew-12 gone, the port is clear for CRS-35, a cargo Dragon carrying the final pair of ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays. NASA is holding a post-splashdown teleconference at 1:15 p.m. ET covering both the crew’s return and the upcoming cargo launch.

SpaceX is buying 800 MHz spectrum from Grain to turn Starlink Mobile into a carrier.
SpaceX has agreed to buy a nationwide block of low band wireless spectrum, a deal the company says will let Starlink Mobile operate as a full US carrier rather than a satellite add-on for someone else’s network.
The company announced the agreement on X on Thursday afternoon, saying it will “pave the way for @Starlink to become a major mobile carrier in the US.” The seller is Grain Management, a private investment firm that confirmed in a statement that SpaceX will acquire 100% of its nationwide 800 MHz portfolio. That covers up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum in the 817 to 824 MHz and 862 to 869 MHz bands. Neither side disclosed a price, and the deal still needs FCC approval.

With this new spectrum and our Gen2 constellation, Starlink Mobile can ensure Americans have access to high-speed mobile broadband no matter where they are → https://t.co/1Uaf48v5pm
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 8, 2026
Grain only recently picked up the licenses itself. It bought the portfolio from T-Mobile in a transaction that closed in August, paying cash plus its own 600 MHz spectrum. Rival AST SpaceMobile had been testing satellites on the same bands before SpaceX stepped in.
SpaceX said its 2 GHz spectrum will handle high bandwidth capacity, while the new 800 MHz layer “ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings.” The company added that most existing phones already support the band, so customers would not need new hardware to use it.
That 2 GHz spectrum came from SpaceX’s EchoStar acquisition last year , which gave the company exclusive S band rights in the US and global Mobile Satellite Service licenses. The Grain spectrum is different in an important way: it is tailored for service from ground towers, not satellites. SpaceX said that combination would make Starlink Mobile “the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum.”
The announcement also follows a key regulatory win. Earlier this week, the FCC approved SpaceX’s plan to deploy 15,000 second generation Starlink Mobile satellites, which the company has said will carry up to 100 times the data density of the current system, as Teslarati previously reported .
Shares of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile fell in extended trading after the announcement. T-Mobile is currently SpaceX’s launch partner for Starlink Mobile in the US, which makes its position the most complicated of the three.
SpaceX has not been subtle about its plans. During the company’s August earnings call, President and COO Gwynne Shotwell said she expected Starlink Mobile to win over customers from the major carriers . “I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers because I think our service will be better,” she said, pointing to dead zone coverage and resilience during disasters. Shotwell also described plans for low cost cellular base stations that could pair with existing Starlink dishes.
SpaceX has targeted 2027 for deployment of its next generation Starlink Mobile satellites, with upgraded service expected by the end of that year. The FCC review of the Grain deal now determines when the terrestrial half of that network can come online.

Just when you thought the sun might be taking a breather, it's unleashed another powerful eruption — and the northern lights forecast just got even more promising.
A fourth coronal mass ejection (CME) erupted from the sun on Oct. 8, during a powerful M-class solar flare from the restless sunspot region AR4549. That brings the number of CMEs potentially heading Earth's way to four, raising the possibility of further geomagnetic activity and aurora displays over the coming days.
Early analysis suggests the latest CME could potentially catch up with the third CME on its way towards Earth.
NOAA's aurora forecast suggests auroral activity could be enhanced across northern North America. Exactly how far south the aurora might appear remains uncertain and depends on how the incoming CMEs interact with Earth's magnetic field .
G2 geomagnetic storm conditions are forecast for Oct. 9 and during such storms, auroras have previously been observed as far south as New York and Idaho .
While northern U.S. states currently have the best prospects, skywatchers farther south shouldn't completely write off their chances just yet. With multiple CMEs approaching Earth in quick succession, there's still considerable uncertainty over how geomagnetic conditions will develop. If the incoming eruptions interact favorably with Earth's magnetic field, auroras could potentially reach much farther south than currently anticipated.
So if you're at mid-latitudes, make sure those aurora alerts are switched on and your camera batteries are charged. This could be an interesting few days for northern lights enthusiasts!
For real-time forecasts based on your location, consider using a space weather app. A great option is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts" (available for iOS and Android ). For a deeper dive into space weather conditions, "Space Weather Live" is another excellent choice (available for iOS and Android )
NOAA's latest 3-day forecast now places the strongest geomagnetic activity later on Oct. 9 than previously anticipated.
Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions are forecast between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. EDT (1200and 1800 GMT), with moderate (G2) conditions predicted between 2 and 8 p.m. EDT (1800 and midnight GMT) .
Further activity is possible over the weekend, with NOAA currently forecasting minor (G1) conditions between 11 p.m. and 2 a.m. EDT on Oct. 10-11 (0300-0600 GMT Oct. 11).
For those wishing to catch some auroras, the advice remains the same! Keep your aurora alerts switched on and check conditions whenever skies are dark and clear. These forecast windows are not set in stone, particularly when multiple CMEs are involved!
This is where things get complicated.
Current modelling suggests the first CMEs could reach Earth on Oct. 9. Space weather physicist Tamitha Skov notes that the two Oct. 6 CMEs could reach Earth in relatively quick succession, delivering a one-two punch to Earth's magnetic field. However, their journey may be influenced by the surrounding solar wind , making precise arrival times difficult to pin down.
The third CME could follow late Oct. 10 or early Oct. 11 (UTC), potentially prolonging unsettled geomagnetic activity and aurora prospects into the weekend.
And now there's a fourth CME to consider. Early analysis suggests this latest eruption is traveling faster than some of its predecessors, raising the possibility that it could catch up with the third CME before reaching Earth. The 'cannibal CME' could further complicate the timings and strength of resulting geomagnetic activity. And remember, even an Earth-directed CME doesn't guarantee a spectacular aurora display. Much will depend on how the magnetic fields carried by these eruptions interact with Earth's magnetic field when they arrive.
With AR4549 still magnetically complex and facing Earth, more solar activity could be on the way. The sun sure is keeping us on our toes this week!

DUNLOW, W.Va. — Bill Likens stared down a half-mile-long line of cars that started forming before the sun came up over the Appalachian Mountains. He had one job: figure out how to feed them all.
Some had driven more than 30 miles in aging cars and trucks that wheezed down flood-prone roads through the steep hills. They sat silently as the temperature rose into the 80s, their vehicles turned off with no air conditioning to preserve gas, waiting hours for a few boxes of food.
Aided by a cane, Likens, 51, surveyed the pallets being unloaded off a semitruck that arrived that morning. He counted cartons of eggs and sacks of potatoes to calculate how much each waiting car could get — an algorithm of hunger he is constantly trying to solve.
“There’s a decent chance we could run out,” said Likens, who runs the food pantry in Dunlow as director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, a small brick church he attended growing up.
“I don’t want them to sit in that line and not get anything,” he said. “But I don’t have a lot of extra food these days.”
Increasingly, the job of feeding the nation’s hungry is falling on the shoulders of everyday Americans like Likens, who have become the last bulwark against hunger in a land of plenty.
Likens and others on the front lines of feeding their neighbors say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. Food distribution programs are getting less food from federal programs to feed the hungry after cuts by the Trump administration. At the same time, restrictions on food stamps from the Republicans’ “big, beautiful bill” have driven up demand, while rising gas prices because of the Iran war have cut into the budgets of households and food banks alike.
The challenges extend far beyond Appalachia. An NBC News survey of 48 of the largest food banks across 35 states and Washington, D.C., found that nearly three-quarters said more people are showing up at their doors over the past year, from workers on their lunch breaks to older adults overwhelmed with medical expenses. At the same time, more than 80% said the food and funding they received through the U.S. Department of Agriculture had dropped and they were struggling with higher fuel costs for transporting food.
In Maine, Good Shepherd Food Bank said the USDA cut the amount of food it received from 13 million pounds to 9 million pounds in one year. A Michigan food bank, Forgotten Harvest, said it’s handing out less food to make sure there is enough to go around: one bag of potatoes instead of two, two tubs of yogurt as opposed to six.
“People are facing multiple hits to their budgets,” said Poonam Gupta, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a think tank that researches social and economic issues. “It is really difficult to find a way to continue affording a healthy and nutritious and balanced diet when you just have these constant hits.”
Food banks’ struggles started in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term when officials cut a $400 million Covid-era program to supply food banks with food from local farmers and paused an estimated $500 million in other planned food purchases by the USDA. Funding from Congress for a separate decades-old program to supply food banks with emergency food assistance has increased over the past several years, but many food bank leaders said they’re still getting less overall than during the Biden administration.
Trump also signed into law the new restrictions on who can receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, or food stamps, requiring nearly all able-bodied adults not caring for young children to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month. Since the law was enacted, more than 5 million people , including at least 1 million children , have lost their food benefits.
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the administration’s policies, saying Trump is “uplifting every American’s financial situation” through tax cuts and efforts to increase jobs and business investments.
“President Trump is strengthening SNAP for the Americans who need it by ensuring these programs are sustainable for future generations,” Kelly said, including measures to “crack down on waste, fraud and abuse.”
The USDA said it hasn’t reduced the amount of food it provides.
“Every day, the Food and Nutrition Administration invests $340 million in low-income communities and people in need of nutrition assistance, including millions of school children, elderly, and the disabled,” a USDA spokesperson said. “The mission to help those in need has not changed.”
While those on the ground say they are thankful for everything they get, they are struggling to do more with less. Facing Hunger Foodbank, which supplies Likens’ pantry and others  across Appalachia, has seen a 25% increase in the number of people seeking help over the past year, while the amount of food the federal government supplies has fallen by a third, CEO Cyndi Kirkhart said.
Those forces have hit especially hard in areas that were already struggling economically, like West Virginia’s once-flourishing coal mining communities. The spike in gas costs means a 45-minute drive to the nearest grocery store can set residents back more than $15. And West Virginians who must comply with the new work requirements to receive food benefits are confronting a lack of jobs and training programs. Since last summer, about 24,000 people, including 8,000 children, have lost food stamps, according to the West Virginia Department of Human Services.
“It’s like the pandemic on steroids without funds,” Kirkhart said. “I don’t believe the government needs to provide everything, but if you’re going to ask us to, please help.”
Likens learned the tricks of how to battle an aching emptiness in his stomach early in life. When he was 12, his father, a construction supervisor for a coal mine, was injured by a falling piece of equipment. Suddenly, his family of seven had to live off of just $350 a month in government assistance.
Growing up, there were days he ate only two meals, and he was never full. His mother often made biscuits and gravy because it was relatively filling. For the first week of the month, she had enough powdered milk to make the gravy. For the rest of the month, she mixed water, oil and a bit of flour. It had the appearance of gravy but not the flavor.
The family survived with help from the same church he works for today. He and his wife, Addie, whom he met playing in the middle school band, live in the church house he and his brothers helped build as teenagers to repay the church for the food it had provided.
In this corner of West Virginia, hunger is nothing new. For decades, the coal mining jobs that built many of the communities here have been leaving; the last mine near Dunlow closed more than a decade ago. Attracting new industries has been a struggle with little flat land, limited internet service and aging infrastructure. As the jobs left, so did many of the area’s younger residents, leaving a large population of seniors, including many raising grandchildren, who rely on Social Security as their only income.
Likens said making sure no one goes hungry in his hometown has never been harder. His pantry, which serves 700 to 800 households, has gotten 25% less food from the USDA over the past several years, he said. The amount varies month to month, making it difficult to plan. In August, he got just 2.5 pounds of food per household, compared with the 20 pounds he was getting monthly several years ago. Meat has become a rarity, replaced by items like dried beans, which can be difficult to cook with for those with disabilities or children preparing their own meals.
“This is the leanest we’ve been in the 23 years I’ve been doing this,” Likens said.

CME FSPI structure official sports statistics into rules-based, benchmark financial metrics. articles.title_orig: A new economic model for the 21st century
articles.title_zh: A new economic model for the 21st century
articles.content_orig:
As the World Bank and IMF reconsider decades of market-led orthodoxy, a deeper debate is emerging over the role of the state, industrial policy and public investment in building resilient, inclusive economies
In the run-up to this year’s International Monetary Fund and World Bank Spring Meetings, the one story that cut through the noise was that the World Bank had embraced industrial policy after decades of advising against it. But while much of the ensuing debate focused on whether this ‘U-turn’ is good or bad, overdue or dangerous, few pondered the fundamental question: What has actually changed?
The World Bank has merely affirmed what many of us have long argued: the framework it has promoted since 1993 – when its East Asian Miracle report cautioned against industrial-policy tools – has not served developing countries well. Such advice, World Bank Chief Economist Indermit Gill recently observed, “has the practical value of a floppy disk today.” Yet in his defence of the report, he also made clear how limited the shift remains. Industrial policy, he argued, should be “targeted and temporary,” an exception to a market-led model, rather than a tool for driving broader economic transformations.
The World Bank’s latest work confirms that industrial policy is more replicable across income levels and institutional contexts than the old consensus admitted, with a toolkit that extends beyond tariffs and subsidies. Public support for private actors, the bank now argues, should come with carrots and sticks, including withdrawal of finance from firms that underperform. This new position aligns with arguments we made in the ‘Entrepreneurial State’ and through more recent work on the role of missions and conditionalities.
But new conclusions do not automatically produce new economics. The World Bank still treats the state as a mere fixer of market failures, rather than as a market creator and shaper. The question is not whether governments should intervene after markets have failed. It is what kind of economy we want to build in the first place. Which public purposes should guide investment, and how can institutions govern the public–private bargain so that value is created collectively and shared fairly?
Viewed in these terms, the bank still falls short, because it treats fiscal-policy space as a fixed constraint within which to optimise, rather than as a set of institutional capacities that can be developed. As a result, the bank would still organise industrial policy only around specific sectors and considerations of comparative advantage. But the energy transition, water and food security, public health, and economic resilience are not sectoral issues. They call for economy-wide missions.
From market fixer to market shaper Nor is the World Bank an isolated case. The IMF’s own economists have similarly documented how austerity and liberalisation fail to deliver. Yet these findings have yet to translate consistently into new operational practices. That needs to change. The IMF and the World Bank sit at the centre of an international order whose default advice still reflects an economics not supported by real-world evidence. What they model, measure and recommend shapes how development and macroeconomic policy are done around the world. They help determine who has access to liquidity, and on what terms; whose debt is treated as sustainable; whose public investment is seen as credible; and whose policy autonomy is constrained. The wealthy countries that fund and control these institutions are not exempt from the consequences of the same economics. For decades, the same flawed assumptions shaped policy in Europe and the US, suppressing public investment, weakening public services, treating wages as costs rather than as fuel for aggregate demand and leaving households exposed to shocks that markets failed to manage. The resulting affordability crisis has now become a political one. The economics that constrained development policy abroad – hollowing out public capacity and narrowing what governments can do – helped fuel the far right at home. Europe’s response to the 2022 energy shock shows what is at stake. From 2022 to 2025, EU member states and the UK incurred $1.8trn in additional costs, much of it absorbed by households and public budgets, while the shareholders of firms charging higher prices benefited. Spain points to an alternative. Having invested in energy security as a mission, rather than as a subsidy category, it now generates more than half of its electricity from renewables, leaving it more insulated than its neighbours from the latest energy shock.
Consistent framework required Making such resilience the default, rather than the exception, requires an economic framework that governments can apply consistently. The Global Progressive Mobilisation, convened by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, recently brought together progressive governments from around the world to start shaping a new economic consensus.
Its foundations are clear. We need public institutions with the capacity to invest, coordinate, and govern markets in the public interest. We need finance designed around missions, not leverage ratios, and policy frameworks that treat fiscal space not as a market-determined ceiling, but as something built by productive investment. And we need measures of value orientated around the common good. The argument for a new economics is being won. Now we must show what comes next.

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle pressed a MAGA donor for $100,000 to pay American Express , according to a report.
The Wall Street Journal , citing text messages between Donald Trump Jr’s ex and Eric Deters, a Kentucky attorney and former congressional candidate, says she made the plea days before her confirmation hearing in July 2025.
Deters, 63, also a co-founder of the regional restaurant chain Snappy Tomato Pizza, had been looking to Guilfoyle for help resolving his tax and legal issues with the Internal Revenue Service , as well as on netting an appearance on Tucker Carlson ’s podcast and on getting a song he wrote to Kid Rock , according to the Journal , which presented a series of images showing the alleged texts.
“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she texted Deters via Signal on July 3, per the Journal , adding a praying emoji and a PDF containing payment instructions from Amex.
“You could just send it here. It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that’s all that will show. Please.”
“Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work,” he reportedly replied. “I can’t do this without getting a divorce.”
“I’ve been calling you for over a week straight,” Guilfoyle answered. “You could be here meeting with Billy Long.”
Long had been appointed Commissioner for the IRS that June but was fired by President Donald Trump in August .
Deters declined to pay the money and told the Journal Guilfoyle had promised him that if he did, “I will be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever,” but, in the end, “never came through on anything.”
At several points in the exchanges cited by the Journal , she appeared to express concerns about a potential paper trail.
“Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” she said in one. “It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on signal.”
“What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” she added in another.
Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the newspaper the ambassador disputed the authenticity of the messages but did not offer specifics.
On a trip to Greece, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was aware of the Journal ’s report but had no idea if it was true and said he would not address it.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel,” he said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.
“It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things.”
A U.S. Embassy official told the Journal : “Guilfoyle’s career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values.
“She was fully vetted by the bipartisan Senate Foreign Relations Committee and confirmed by the U.S. Senate. The ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity.”

Deters said he had first met Guilfoyle when he founded a Covid-era event in Kentucky called Freedom Fest and paid her $300,000 to speak alongside other members of the Trump family.
He also donated $125,000 to a pro-Trump PAC in 2022, according to Federal Election Commission records cited by the Journal.

articles.title_orig: Aaron Sorkin warns of Facebook's recklessness in 'The Social Reckoning'
articles.title_zh: Aaron Sorkin warns of Facebook's recklessness in 'The Social Reckoning'
articles.content_orig:
Jeremy Strong plays Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning. Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures Entertainment hide caption
A decade after telling Facebook's origin story in The Social Network , Aaron Sorkin returns to familiar terrain by sounding the alarm on some of the collateral damage caused in more recent years by a company that now counts an estimated three billion users worldwide.
In The Social Reckoning , out in theaters this week, the fictionalized Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg is squarely focused on the company's growth, rather literally at all costs.
"There's supposed to be some kind of tension between growth and safety. He's abandoned the safety part, and it's just about growth," Sorkin told Morning Edition host A Martínez.
Aaron Sorkin, right, wrote and directed The Social Reckoning , 16 years after his Academy-winning turn as screenwriter of The Social Network , which told Facebook's origin story. Jeremy Strong, left, plays the role of company co-founder Mark Zuckerberg in the latest film. Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures Entertainment hide caption
As a result, real-life whistleblower Frances Haugen has said, the social media network allowed hate speech, violence and misinformation to spread at a far greater pace than it was letting on.
Haugen's findings initially came to light in 2021 through then-Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz's investigative series, The Facebook Files . Haugen also took the unusual step of going public around the same time. In the wake of the ensuing outcry, Facebook's parent company rebranded itself as Meta .
The tech giant also said it reduced political content on Facebook feeds and gave users more control over what they see on the platform. In response to NPR's requests, Meta declined to comment on The Social Reckoning , which remains a work of biographical fiction .
Sorkin's film was inspired in part by Horwitz's book recounting the ordeal, Broken Code . Haugen (played by Mickey Madison) evolves from passionate Facebook employee to audacious whistleblower as she interacts with Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White).
Horwitz found that in 2018, Facebook changed its newsfeed algorithm so that resharing or replying to a post was weighted up to 30 times as much as a standard "like," while comments were worth 15 times as much and an emoji response was worth five times as much.
"Facebook did this knowing that the thing you're most likely to re-share is anything that makes you angry — rage bait. So in addition to the enormous amount of misinformation they are pumping into the air supply, they are also purposely giving you content that they hope will make you angry," Sorkin said.
While preparing The Social Network — which earned him a Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar — and The Social Reckoning , Sorkin created a dummy Facebook account to try it out himself.
Mikey Madison, right, plays Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen in Aaron Sorkin's, left, The Social Reckoning . Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures Entertainment hide caption
After the newsfeed showed him a picture of a dachshund, Sorkin kept clicking on similar content, aware he was training the algorithm to his liking.
"For the next two years, my entire feed was filled with pictures of dachshunds, which I find harmless. So my Facebook page wasn't dangerous at all. It was pictures of cute dogs," he said. "But if, like 43% of adults [Facebook users], you use Facebook as your source of news , you're in deep trouble."
Jesse Eisenberg's turn as Zuckerberg in The Social Network was so visceral that he was often conflated with the tech entrepreneur and fans would walk up to him in public quoting lines from the film.
Jeremy Allen White, left, plays then-Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, who authored a series of landmark investigative stories known as the Facebook Files based on a massive leak of internal Facebook documents. Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures Entertainment hide caption
Sorkin naturally reached out to him first for The Social Reckoning , which Sorkin both writes and directs. But Eisenberg refused the role.
"It turns out Jesse Eisenberg no longer wants to be conflated with Mark Zuckerberg. He doesn't like the guy," Sorkin said. The night of the 2025 Academy Awards ceremony, he had also told Jeremy Strong of the upcoming project, and Strong had asked to be considered if Eisenberg turns down the role.
"So I got that lucky, we replaced Joe DiMaggio with Mickey Mantle," said Sorkin. "Anyone who's seen Jeremy's work at this point, whether it's in Succession or The Apprentice , here on Broadway, you know that he's going to blow the doors off the place — best American actor under 50 years old."
Strong's stiff, unemotional body language is an uncanny echo of Zuckerberg's public appearances. "But it's not about the impersonation, it's really about what's going on behind his eyes," Sorkin said.
Writer/director Aaron Sorkin, right, calls Jeremy Strong, right, "the best American actor under 50 years old." Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures Entertainment hide caption
This month, the writer-director's career breakthrough A Few Good Men is back on Broadway for its first-ever revival. The courtroom drama was first staged in 1989 before Rob Reiner turned it into a film released three years later.
But Sorkin insists his creative tank runs on empty after major projects.
"I am the living embodiment of Sisyphus. This movie, it opens October 9th. And on October 10th, I will be back at the bottom of the mountain," he said.
"I'll be banging my head against the wall and thinking, I may have written the last thing I'm going to write. I've used all the words I know in every order I can think of... So I'm girding myself for that terrible feeling."
Margaux Bauerlein produced the broadcast version of this story.

Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder helped celebrate Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday at the leader's home, the Kremlin said on Thursday.
Pictures posted on Telegram showed Schroeder and Putin smiling broadly and shaking hands, with an old-style stove and a Russian samovar used to boil water for tea in the background.
"Vladimir Putin found out from the morning news the day before that Gerhard Schroeder was in Moscow and had come on business for the company Globus," the Kremlin said on Telegram.
"The president invited his old friend to his home. Gerhard Schroeder was with Vladimir Putin when the head of state celebrated his birthday yesterday."
Schroeder, who served as chancellor from 1998 to 2005, recently joined the supervisory board of Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus. He visited one of its Moscow stores on Wednesday and was greeted with applause from employees, Russian TV footage showed.
Schroeder has faced criticism, notably in Germany, over his links to Russian business and Putin, ties that have persisted despite Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and subsequent waves of Western sanctions.
Putin suggested in May that Schroeder could represent European countries in peace talks to settle the conflict.
European foreign ministers rejected the notion of any such role for Schroeder.
