articles.title_orig: Experience: I became the world’s oldest crowd surfer at 99
articles.title_zh: Experience: I became the world’s oldest crowd surfer at 99
articles.content_orig:
After retiring at 83, I had a new lease of life creating social media content with my grandson. Then I broke the crowd surfing world record
I n 2013, aged 87, I was playing basketball with my grandson Ross in Ohio while he was home from college. He made a video of me blocking his shot, posted it online, and people really ate it up. We started doing comedy skits together and now have more than 4 million followers on Instagram.
After doing lots of short videos, we decided to make a documentary about my life. As part of it, we compiled my bucket list. One of the things I wanted to do was break a world record. Ross and I spent months thinking of something that would be outrageous, but also fun and inclusive. We settled on me becoming the world’s oldest crowd surfer.
Ross knows the country singer Brantley Gilbert, and he was willing to help us at a show he was playing in Bellville, Texas. Originally, during the crowd surfing, I was going to be strapped to a board Ross had made to protect my back, but it was flexing too much, so he strapped me into a stretcher instead.
I was 99 years and 274 days old the day it happened. It was the first time I’d ever crowd surfed. To break the record, I had to stay up for at least 10 seconds. There were 20,000 people in the crowd – we planned for them to move me in a straight line from the back to the front. But 20 minutes before we were due to start, we saw that everyone in the main crowd was sitting in chairs with gaps between them. Ross started panicking. We used the mosh pit instead, and I travelled in a U-shape from stage right to stage left.
I wore a white T-shirt with a red outline of my face on it so I would stand out from the crowd. Brantley introduced me and said: “I’ll beat you up if you drop Granny.”
I was launched out and I felt as if I was flying. I knew I had to trust everyone. Ross panicked because there was a walkway between both sides of the stage with a 10ft gap and a high fence that I had to be passed over. He jumped the fence as I went across and security people carried me over. I was held up for more than three minutes – nearly an entire song. I was so content. I put my arms out and felt I could touch the sky.
after newsletter promotion
When I got back on the stage, the crowd chanted, “Granny, Granny”. I stood there, soaking it all in. It gave me chills. I was recognised by Guinness World Records for becoming the oldest person to crowd surf at a concert .
Ross comes up with all the ideas. He says he’s Steven Spielberg and I’m Betty White. I only realised how much people liked our videos when I went to the grocery store one day and people were asking to take pictures with me.
This is a whole new life for me. I grew up on a farm in Ohio, the youngest of seven children. We didn’t have TV or a phone. We had chores to do from a young age. During the second world war, I made ammunition in a weapons factory, and I worked in factories until my retirement at 83. I’ve worked hard – it gave me purpose.
The videos are a new kind of work. Meeting people is my favourite part. I’ve met Pope Leo and celebrities like Tom Holland and Bad Bunny on red carpets. I love meeting people who know us from social media. They come up to me and say: “I was lonely and sad in hospital and I watched your videos to lift me up.” People say they’ve reconnected with family after watching Ross and I together. When I’m on my deathbed, I want to know that we made everybody’s day a little better.
I took care of Ross when he was a baby, but this has brought us closer. Before, I only saw him a handful of times a year, but now we live together in Ohio.
I turned 100 this summer, and I had two parties with hundreds of people. I can’t believe I’m 100. I’m the only one out of my siblings who has lived this long. Not all days are peachy. The hardest part of getting older is the aches and pains. Making our videos gives me a purpose, and that boosts me on days I don’t feel so good.
I hope our videos make people realise that it’s never too late to live your best life. If you want to do something new, do it now. Enjoy every moment, because it goes by in the blink of an eye.

articles.title_orig: Finland: The world's happiest nation faces a glum winter
articles.title_zh: Finland: The world's happiest nation faces a glum winter
articles.content_orig:
There's an uneasy mood in Finland , the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.
With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.
Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.
Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.
Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.
The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.
Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.
"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.
Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.

To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.
While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.
Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."
While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.
With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.
"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.
Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.
Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.
During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war , the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.
While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.
On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.
Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.
On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.
Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

articles.title_orig: A Nobel for chiral catalysts’ helping hand
articles.title_zh: A Nobel for chiral catalysts’ helping hand
articles.content_orig:
By Phillip Broadwith 2026-10-09T08:05:00+01:00
The 2026 Nobel prize in chemistry has been awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai , ‘for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis’. The prize recognises the pair’s contribution to understanding the very fundamentals of how we can influence and control the handedness of chiral molecules.
Asymmetric synthesis is a cornerstone of modern drug development, as well as being important for flavours, fragrances and agrochemicals. But chiral molecules also crop up in liquid crystals, polymers and optical materials, as well as across various classes of speciality chemicals. Almost all these products rely, at some point, on catalysts that can transform achiral or racemic molecules into products in which one enantiomer is massively – if not exclusively – dominant.
Source: © Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images
This year’s prize recognises truly fundamental science that has had huge bearing on the commercial applications of asymmetric catalysis
When you’re aiming to make chiral molecules for commercial sale, an efficient synthesis has a significant effect on cost – and hence profitability. Cleaner reactions mean less wasted materials, as well as less time and resources spent on separation and purification. Understanding how to create more effective catalysts, which can drive higher yields and selectivity, can translate into a huge competitive advantage.
Henri Kagan and his team’s insight into the intricacies of how catalysts can be manipulated to drastically improve their performance underlies all this development. Likewise, there are different approaches to enantio-enrichment, as Kenso Soai and his team’s autocatalytic experiments showed.
This year’s laureates didn’t invent asymmetric synthesis, but filled in some key aspects in our understanding of how it works and how we can do it better. This fundamental research has naturally stimulated many other researchers to ask further questions, digging deeper into how these reactions work and further advancing our understanding of chirality and catalysis.
That, in turn, shows up in the applications: new and better catalyst systems have allowed us to build ever more complex molecules in more efficient ways, and directly enabled the wide commercial availability of chiral reagents and chemical building blocks. A fact that’s worth remembering next time you’re browsing through a catalogue, planning your next synthesis.

articles.title_orig: Made in Nebraska: Combines built for the world
articles.title_zh: Made in Nebraska: Combines built for the world
articles.content_orig:
CNH builds the Case IH Axial-Flow series and 260 series combines at its manufacturing plant along Highway 281 in Grand Island, Neb.
Andy Dozler grew up on a farm near Albion, Neb., operating red Case IH equipment in his family’s fields. And yes, he does bleed Case IH red.
Today, when Dozler is driving down the road and sees a Case IH AF series combine — voted in 2025 as the “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” — working in the field, he can say with great pride that his team and at the Case IH manufacturing plant in Grand Island, Neb., built that combine.
In fact, at that plant, they build Case IH AF series and 260 series combines that are sold around the globe, with each combine individually customized for a specific location and buyer.
For Dozler, this is his dream job. After graduating from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, he took a job with CNH, the parent company of Case IH, as a quality engineer. He spent a little over a year at the New Holland, Pa., plant, where he worked on the round baler, square baler and pull-type silage chopper.
He started at the Grand Island plant in 2006, working his way up through the engineering department. Today, Dozler is the manufacturing engineering manager at the plant, leading a team of 20 engineers and six tool-and-die operators. And he gets to be on the ground level of researching, developing and building Case IH combines and other farm equipment for the world.
Andy Dozler, an Albion, Neb., native and University of Nebraska-Lincoln graduate, serves as the manufacturing engineering manager at the Case IH plant in Grand Island. He was involved in the development of the new Case IH AF series combines that won the 2025 “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” award last fall.
During a recent plant tour, Dozler told Nebraska Farmer that his engineering team was intimately involved in the development of the revolutionary AF series combines. Exploration for the development of a Class 10+ combine started as far back as 2011 for Case IH.
The first prototype was built in 2013, and by 2023, a combine was built in a special bay at the Grand Island plant. The first commercial AF combine rolled off the assembly line in March 2024.
For the AF9, AF10 and AF11, the grain tank capacity ranges from 455 bushels up to 567 bushels, and the unload rate goes from 4.5 bushels per second up to 6 bushels per second. With a feeder width of 56 inches, and peak horsepower ranging in the series from 635 hp up to 775 hp, these combines have more capacity than any other Case IH combine made to date.
It was all part of the plan as the new models were developed, Dozler said, as he described the responsibilities of his engineering team at the plant.
“Our team consists of advanced manufacturing engineers who support future programs, as well as assembly, weld, test, fabrication and tool design engineers,” he said. “Our tool-and-die operators are responsible for building new tools and fixtures, as well as repairing and reworking existing fixtures.”
On the manufacturing engineering side, their highest responsibility is to keep the production lines running. “We accomplish this by quickly addressing fit-up issues, quality concerns and missing-part situations,” Dozler said.
They also review design changes, determining how those changes will affect the plant, and develop the bills of materials required to build the products and determine the tooling and equipment needed — including torque tools, weld fixtures and assembly equipment. They figure out crucial timing and sequence for implementing engineering changes on the production lines.
With each combine produced at the plant, whether that is a 260 or AF series, the engineers determine where parts and processes should be incorporated into the production lines and ensure the lines remain properly balanced.
“Our team continuously works on quality improvement, safety and cost-reduction projects,” Dozler added. “Overall, our manufacturing engineering plays a key role in supporting current production while preparing the plant for future products and process changes.”
Combines aren’t the only pieces of new farm machinery rolling out of Grand Island. The plant builds Case IH windrowers, disk headers and sicklebar headers, along with New Holland bale wagons and self-propelled windrowers.
Farmers who purchase new Case IH combines can tour the plant in Grand Island, Neb., watch their own combine as it is built, start their combine for the first time and even drive it off the production line.
The plant was opened as Sperry New Holland in 1965. After years of expansion and corporate acquisitions, the 165-acre site in Grand Island — which includes a main campus of three manufacturing buildings and a warehouse north of the plant — has produced a myriad of forage and harvest equipment. It continues to employ hundreds of workers, shipping farm equipment to 34 countries.
Dozler said that plenty of farmers tour the plant and watch their own new combine as it is built at the factory. This experience includes the culmination of being able to start the machine for the first time and even drive it off the production line.
Watching satisfied customers is one of the great joys Dozler receives from his job, along with the thrill of watching those combines made in Grand Island in the field bringing in another harvest.
The competition for “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” is sponsored by the Nebraska Manufacturing Alliance, with support from Pinnacle Bank. In this March Madness-style tournament, voters decide which nominated inventions and products advance to the finals.
Every year, agriculture takes a center stage spot in the voting, with Valley center pivots taking the prize in 2024 and the Case IH AF series combine winning in 2025. Voting for the 2026 winners closed Oct. 4.
Learn more at nemanufacturingalliance.com .
senior editor of Nebraska Farmer, Nebraska Farmer
Curt Arens began writing about Nebraska’s farm families when he was in high school. Before joining Farm Progress first as a field editor in 2010, and then as editor of Nebraska Farmer in 2021, he had worked as a freelance farm writer for 27 years for newspapers and farm magazines, including Nebraska Farmer. His real full-time career during this period was farming his family’s fourth-generation land near Crofton, Neb., where his family raised corn, soybeans, wheat, oats, alfalfa, cattle, hogs and Christmas trees.
Curt and his wife, Donna, have four children: Lauren, Taylor, Zachary and Benjamin. They are active in their church and St. Rose School in Crofton, where Donna teaches. The family now rents out their crop ground to a neighbor, but still lives on the same farm first operated by Curt's great-grandparents. The family runs a few cows and other assorted 4-H and FFA critters.
Previously, the 1986 University of Nebraska animal science graduate wrote a weekly rural life column, developed a farm radio program and wrote books about farm life. He received media honors from the Nebraska Forest Service, Center for Rural Affairs, Nebraska Association of County Extension Boards and Nebraska Association of Natural Resources Districts.
He wrote about the spiritual side of farming in his 2008 book, Down to Earth: Celebrating a Blessed Life on the Land , garnering a Catholic Press Association award.

Microsoft bundled its AI-powered Office features into Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscriptions last year , but it only allowed the primary account holder to access the AI benefits. Now, Microsoft is about to let Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers share Copilot and AI usage features, alongside access to Office apps and OneDrive storage, with up to five other people on a plan.
In an email to Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers seen by The Verge , Microsoft outlines the changes that are coming to subscription plans over the coming months:
The storage changes seem like the major downside to Microsoft’s updates. Instead of getting 1TB of OneDrive storage per account, Microsoft is now limiting this to just 2TB of shared storage across the entire plan. Microsoft argues this makes storage more flexible if one member exceeds 1TB, but it looks like it’s an easy way for the company to upsell more OneDrive storage in reality.
According to a support note , “Existing subscribers in eligible markets might also qualify for transitional bonus storage.” Microsoft is also planning to provide support to families that use a lot of storage
The changes are being announced a year after Microsoft 365 Premium launched , which offers all the benefits of a Copilot Pro and a Microsoft 365 Family subscription for $19.99 a month. The “more flexible AI usage” change could mean that some subscribers end up paying more for AI usage, depending on how they’re using Copilot.

articles.title_zh: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.content_orig:
© World Economic Forum / Benedikt von Loebell
The World Bank and IMF are shifting away from explicit climate action towards resilience, reflecting political pressure from the US that weakens their response to global heating, argues Federico Sibaja  and Jon Sward.
The authors criticise the World Bank’s approach after its financing supported a Nepal hydropower project that was damaged by devastating floods despite warnings and the absence of a proper climate-risk assessment.
Meanwhile, IMF-backed austerity and fossil-fuel policies in countries including Ecuador and Pakistan are limiting investment in climate adaptation and, in some cases, undermining the shift to renewable energy.
With climate-vulnerable countries facing mounting damage, the authors argue that institutions must expand grant-based finance and debt relief, and ensure climate risks are built into lending decisions and economic programmes.
In a recent interview with the New York Times , World Bank President Ajay Banga explained that the bank wants to avoid the “emotional” debate around climate change and instead focus on resilient investments.
For the leader of an institution that describes itself as the “knowledge bank”, such a desire to skirt the realities of climate science is of course the result of political calculus.
The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, has also shifted gears in recent years: she went from calling for an end to “business as usual” at COP28 , to agreeing with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the need to refocus away from climate change. She has also cut the budget earmarked for climate work by 27%.
Meanwhile, Bessent has questioned the cause of global warming and referred to climate action at global financial institutions as driven by “elite beliefs” .
The World Bank and IMF’s change in approach comes as no surprise, as there is a potentially steep cost of them falling afoul of their largest shareholder, amid its wider war on multilateralism.
But what’s been less discussed is the wider cost of the Bretton Woods institutions’ failure to act in the midst of an accelerating climate emergency – of which the serious flooding in Bangkok, where the World Bank and IMF convene their annual meetings next week, is a stark reminder.
After a prolonged debate on the future of the bank’s climate commitments in the Spring, a compromise was reached in June , when it extended its climate change action plan (CCAP) “indefinitely”, but retired its 45% climate finance target.
As the US’s anti-climate action agenda has cast a long shadow at the institution and elsewhere since last year, bank officials increasingly say their goal is to deliver resilient investments, echoing Banga’s recent statements.
However, there are serious questions about whether the bank’s approach is advancing its aim.
The recent flood disaster in Nepal, which killed more than 1,450 people (with around 5,800 still missing), also damaged 13 hydropower projects, including the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant. Alongside other lenders , Trishuli was backed by financing from the World Bank’s private investment arm , IFC, and a US$87.4mn guarantee from its political risk arm, MIGA. Yet, despite repeated warnings from an independent expert panel, no climate and disaster risk assessment had been properly undertaken as of 2024.
The World Bank needs to ensure that “resilience” is more than an empty signifier. This means having mechanisms in place across all lending instruments to evaluate whether its actions are genuinely leading to positive outcomes for people and the planet, including ex-post assessments of projects that emphasise learning from past mistakes.
It also means rethinking the the bank’s neoliberal era loan conditions in its policy based lending , which have promoted wholesale privatisation in key sectors like energy, and ensuring countries have the policy and fiscal space to pursue green industrial policy .
As evidenced by the Nepal crisis, with the country facing an estimated US$4.7bn in reconstruction costs, climate-vulnerable countries also urgently need a rapid scaling up of grant-based climate finance and debt relief . The World Bank could use its convening role to help move this discussion forward.
The IMF’s relevance has grown due to increasingly frequent shocks to the global economy, such as spikes in fossil fuel prices and extreme weather events. In July 2026 , 30 countries were implementing IMF programmes with conditionalities, and 14 other countries were seeking new arrangements.
Recent analysis has shown that its programmes’ reliance on fiscal consolidation and foreign exchange accumulation can undermine countries’ climate policy goals and put macroeconomic stability – Bessent’s  “focus” of the IMF – at risk. So, while the IMF has become better at diagnosing climate risk, it is also exacerbating it.
For example, in Ecuador, the IMF-backed programme requires primary adjustment of 6.6% of GDP. Such fiscal adjustment can make it harder to invest in climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure. At the same time, the programme explicitly aims to increase oil output.
The same goes for Pakistan. The country has been on the frontlines of the climate crisis in the last few years, with devastating floods in 2022. Yet IMF-backed fiscal consolidation has constrained spending at a time when the country faces enormous adaptation needs. Moreover, reforms in fiscal policy are undermining the energy transition: due to IMF-led energy subsidy removal and tariff increases, the country began a rapid shift to solar, only to see it undermined by IMF-backed higher taxes on solar panels.
Back in June, the IMF’s own independent evaluation office flagged this contradiction. It identified the review of progam design and conditionality , the process through which the institution evaluates the performance of its lending programmes and agrees ways to improve them, as a chance to address it. Yet, when the review wrapped up last month, climate was firmly excluded .
As more countries turn to the IMF to address their vulnerability to shocks, its push for fiscal adjustment and commodity extraction risks accelerating that same vulnerability.
At the upcoming annual meetings, we need to see serious efforts to resolve this contradiction. A good place to start would be the guidance the IMF provides to staff designing loan programmes, which will be developed in the next few months. This must clearly outline under what circumstances climate goals are central to programme success and cannot be ignored.
Without a change of course, the IMF and World Bank will miss a key window of opportunity to stem a runaway climate crisis. In the present context, delaying action is just another form of climate denial.

An economist from the Universidad de Buenos Aires, he is an expert on the interactions between debt and climate policy. He has extensive experience in policymaking, research and campaigning across Argentina, Belgium and internationally.
Jon Sward is environment project manager at the Bretton Woods Project, where he oversees its climate advocacy work towards the World Bank and the IMF. He holds a PhD from the School of Global Studies at the University of Sussex.

articles.title_orig: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.title_zh: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia.
Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race.
Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir.
The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two.
Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution.
The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually.
Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste.
But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes.
In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions.
“Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added.
Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event.
Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others.
This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead.
Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.”
F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.”
Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.”
Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.
Laura Paddison contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt
articles.content_orig:
Attorneys for Christa Pike hold a news conference after a judge ruled the Tennessee Department of Corrections must preserve all evidence related to the failed execution of Pike, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Christa Pike has begun walking and eating again at a hospital a week after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her with lethal drugs, her attorneys said Thursday.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to giver her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn't kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were "limited" and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time.
But the lawyers warned uncertainty remains about her physical recovery and her legal standing after the attempt to carry out her death sentence.
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt.
"While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured," her attorneys said in Thursday's statement. "Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die."
Pike regained consciousness Tuesday and was able to speak after awakening, they said.
They initially described her as "confused" soon after regaining consciousness, and said Thursday that she continued to struggle with concentration and memory. Doctors say it is too early to assess the long-term impacts, the attorneys added.
It also remains unclear whether Tennessee will try to execute her again. Her attorneys have said that they will urge Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole.
"She should never be subjected to another execution attempt," they said in the statement.
Luke Ihnen, attorney for Christa Pike, speaks during a news conference after a judge ruled the Tennessee Department of Corrections must preserve all evidence related to the failed execution of Pike, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Lee has since postponed the state's only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of why the execution failed. The state's prison chief resigned after the execution attempt.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.
Pike's attorneys wrote in a court filing that "apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed."
State officials have offered no explanation of what occurred.
As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

articles.title_orig: Oxford Area High School closed Friday after confirmed case of measles
articles.title_zh: Oxford Area High School closed Friday after confirmed case of measles
articles.content_orig:
OXFORD, Pa. (WPVI) -- The Oxford Area High School in Chester County will be closed Friday after a confirmed case of measles was identified within the school community.
The school district announced the closure in a letter sent to families Thursday.
"We understand that news like this may be concerning for families," the district wrote. "The health and well-being of our students, staff and community are incredibly important to us, and we recognize that receiving this information can raise questions, concerns and uncertainty."
READ MORE | Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades
School officials said the Chester County Health Department will contact anyone believed to have been exposed.
The announcement comes as Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases , with 86 cases reported in Chester County.
Earlier this week, Jeanne Franklin, director of the Chester County Health Department, said officials had been working closely with school nurses and superintendents ahead of the school year because of concerns about measles transmission.
According to the district's letter, anyone who is not vaccinated against measles, or cannot provide proof of vaccination, must stay away from school and school-related activities for 21 days following a potential exposure.
Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air or direct contact.
Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 Fahrenheit, and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek.
Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says.
The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.

articles.title_orig: Plymouth skateboarder heading to World Skate Games aged 60
articles.title_zh: Plymouth skateboarder heading to World Skate Games aged 60
articles.content_orig:
An amateur skateboarder is set to represent his country for the first time almost 50 years after he took up the sport.
Darren Miles, 60, from Plymouth, is to represent Great Britain in the slalom event at the World Skate Games in Paraguay later this month.
Miles will take part in three disciplines as part of the team made up of a mixture of professionals and amateurs.
"When I was 10 I never thought I would be skateboarding at 60 for my country so that's the main attraction," he said.
Miles first became interested in the sport in 1977 in Essex where he "always had a skateboard and always skated around".
In 2020 he "realised he was slowly losing his tricks" and took to slalom, which involves speed skateboarding around cones.
When he heads to the World Skate Games, Miles said he could be up against competitors who are in their 20s as well as those his own age.
He said "to finish and not get disqualified" would be a successful games for him.
"There's a top 16, I don't really anticipate getting into there, but I'll be going there and supporting all the other guys that are racing, because a few of the English guys are in with a good chance," he said.
"I'll be supporting them and just enjoying being at the event."
He said he enjoyed travelling for skateboarding events and the social aspect of the sport was a "big draw" for him.
"Sometimes you get a sport that's what matches your personality and it can be a lot of fun with a shared danger," he said.
"Everybody's been really supportive and I think a little bit amazed."

articles.title_orig: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.title_zh: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.content_orig:
Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America.
Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down.
The question is: what is he able to do with just a few weeks to go before election day - and will it work?
Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues.
The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US.
Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months.
While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline.
David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices.
"Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says.
Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates.
"The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says.
While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel.
"A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said.
The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies.
Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself.
"The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained.
The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said.
"The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion."
The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product.
"If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said.
But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts.
Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns , following pressure from Trump to do so.
De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree".
Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution.
"As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears."
Earlier this week, Trump said he was "thinking about" suspending federal tax on gasoline.
De Haan said the president has also been imploring states to cut state taxes on gasoline and several have done so, including Ohio and Georgia.
State taxes form a "moderate portion" of what consumers pay at the pump, and those reductions have helped reduce prices and national averages, he said.
However, suspending or reducing the federal levy on gasoline would require the cooperation of Congress.
"That may be difficult to obtain ahead of the midterm elections," said De Haan.
It is also a costly measure.
De Haan estimated that in Indiana, which cut its tax on gasoline in May, it has cost the state government $1bn (£760m) in lost revenue.
Trump has also previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.
While that would provide partial relief in the Gulf and Midwest, according to Pearce, he adds it would be of "little benefit" to the Northeast and West Coast.
"The policy risks backfiring because it would result in stockpiling of diesel, and as that storage runs out, refineries would need to cut back on production," he said.
"That would raise prices of other energy products, including gasoline."
De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated".
"The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said.
That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.
Even if those conflicts are resolved, Ruisard said that due to damage to facilities in the Middle East caused by military strikes it would still take production four to six months to return to normal.
"The message to consumers and industry is that regardless of what happens and whether the president is able to successfully negotiate that kind of a deal," he said.
"High prices are here to stay for a little while at least."

Not long ago I criticized the likes of Apple , Google and Samsung for being lazy; for producing flagship phones with minimal improvements to camera hardware, year after year. By contrast, Chinese brands like Oppo , Vivo and Xiaomi are continually upping the ante in this area, the most obvious example being bespoke teleconverter lenses, such as the Oppo Hasselblad 300mm Explorer Teleconverter .
But there’s another Chinese phone manufacturer we in the West tend to overlook now: Huawei . Ever since Google banned Huawei from accessing Google Mobile Services in 2019, the brand all but died in the US and Europe, but it continues to thrive in its Chinese homeland. So much so that it's just launched what is quite possibly the most audacious piece of camera hardware for a phone I've ever seen.
Not content with simply copying Oppo or Vivo by offering another fixed focal length telephoto lens, Huawei has produced a lens for a camera phone that boasts 10x continuous optical zoom, equating to a 24-240mm focal range (in full-frame terms), plus you get a respectable f/2-4.5 max aperture.
And if that wasn't impressive enough, Huawei has teamed the lens with its own, dedicated 1-inch-type, 50-megapixel RYYB image sensor. This is capable of ISO6400 maximum sensitivity, 4K/60p video recording, and up 960fps slow motion video capture.
The result is the Ruiying Z10: an entire camera attachment that can be mounted directly to the camera island of a Huawei Mate 90 Pro Max, or Mate 90 RS phone - no intermediary case or separate mounting system required. The Z10 takes over all camera hardware duties from the phone, leaving the phone to handle image processing, the control interface, and image preview.
Sure, at approximately 80mm x 70mm in size and weighing 346g, the Z10 is a chunky piece of kit. But it's not unreasonably bulky: the Oppo Hasselblad 300mm Explorer Teleconverter is even heavier at 400g, and let's face it, none of these big lens attachments are going to fit in a jeans' pocket anyway. You really need to think of the Z10 not as an add-on lens you take out with you on a daily basis, but as a camera converter. It gives you the option to turn your phone into a full-on camera with genuine, continuous 10x optical zoom. No switching between your phone’s own individual camera modules and getting varied image quality as a result. No relying on AI zoom, with its sometimes sketchy interpretation of reality.
For everyday use you'd shoot with the cameras in the Mate 90 Pro Max or Mate 90 RS, and that'd be no hardship, as these phones are imaging powerhouses in their own right. We're talking a main camera with a 1/1.28-inch, 50MP sensor and an f/1.4-f/4.0 variable aperture lens, a 200-megapixel 4x periscope telephoto module, also using a 1/1.28-inch sensor, and a 40-megapixel ultrawide camera. But for holidays, events, or other special occasions when you might otherwise want a 'proper' camera, you'd simply attach the Z10 and away you go.

And the price for all this versatility? RMB 5,999, or around $895 US. Sure, that's far from cheap - the same money would buy you a 256GB Pixel 11 phone. But let's consider the alternative: you already have a high-end phone, but also want a dedicated compact camera with a 1-inch sensor and at least 10x optical zoom. An obvious choice would be the Panasonic ZS300/TZ300 , which costs $897, and while this does have 15x zoom reach, I'd bet my left arm its image quality won't be as impressive as that from the Mate 90/Ruiying Z10 combo.
But sadly I'm ignoring the elephant in the room here: the Ruiying Z10 looks incredible, it'll probably perform very well, but unless you live in China, you'll never actually get the chance to find out. Who could have predicted in 2019, when the US was doing its best to kill off Huawei's consumer phone division, that in 2026 the brand wouldn't just be prospering in this sector, it'd be at the cutting edge of camera phone innovation.

articles.title_orig: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
articles.title_zh: Fiery Senate Debates in Maine, Michigan and Georgia: Five Takeaways
articles.content_orig:
Candidates traded personal attacks and clashed over a range of issues in closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday, with control of Congress at stake
With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake.
In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority.
Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates.
Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms.
“Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative.
Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth.
“Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.”
Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported.
Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices.
Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill.
In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins.
“Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said.
He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.”
Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views.
“You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.”
Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”.
Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada.
This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor , saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now.
During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said.
El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”.
“He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.”
In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.”
Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran.
But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war.
She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”.
“You owe me an apology,” she said.
In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state.
“Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.”
He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022 . Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate.
In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide.
Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups.
“He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both.
But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.”
He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.”

HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii News Now interviewed U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda and state Sen. Brenton Awa, candidates for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District, about the Iran war, aid to Israel and immigration enforcement.
Awa said he is seeking only one term in Congress.
“I only want to go for two years, one term, and the reason is, is because I don’t care about all of those world policies and all the votes that’ll have to be taken. I’ll have to care when I am taking it,” Awa said.
Awa said he wants money spent on the Iran war and support for Israel to instead go to American families dealing with disaster.
“But my biggest focus, if we’re going to send billions of dollars to Israel or another country, my only concern is why isn’t that money coming to Hawaii,” Awa said.
Tokuda said ending the war is the best way to reduce energy costs. She opposes aid to Israel because of its treatment of Palestinians.
“It’s a genocide,” Tokuda said.
“When you take a look at the weapons they are using, it was our weapons, which is why I voted against funding weapons sales to Israel for now, because that is blood on our hands,” Tokuda said.
On immigration enforcement, Awa does not oppose mass deportation but said he believes ICE has been too violent.
“The idea is good. The way they go and carry it out, and I don’t know,” Awa said. “I’m not there on the ground, so I don’t know, but other than what I see, through you guys, the media. But when you see people dying, there is no way that that should ever happen.”
Tokuda said there will be pressure to fix immigration laws after the election.
“We absolutely have to pass some kind of meaningful bipartisan immigration reform that protects our borders, that creates legal pathways to citizenship and doesn’t result in Americans getting executed in our streets,” Tokuda said.
Awa acknowledges the odds are stacked against him in a district that has never elected a Republican, and GOP voters have been discouraged by President Trump’s unpopularity.
Awa did not have to give up his Senate seat to run for Congress and has two years remaining on his term.

This year’s flu season started months early and in an unexpected part of the country, according to health officials.
The unusually early start to the season has prompted local health officials to urge people to get their flu shots as soon as possible.
In Los Angeles County, flu activity began rising in September, ahead of its typical early-November start, Dr. Dawn Terashita told The Times on Wednesday.
That isn’t a major surprise, said Terashita, associate director of the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health’s Acute Communicable Disease Control Program. Flu tends to be “very unpredictable,” she said, due to the ways that it mutates.
But another unusual factor was that the flu season started this year in the Western states.
Typically, the flu starts in the South, then makes its way across the country, according to Dr. Elizabeth Hudson, regional chief of infectious diseases at Kaiser Permanente Southern California.
Terashita said it’s too soon to know the reason behind this phenomenon.
Given the early flu surge, Hudson said in a statment it might have caught people off-guard, as many hadn’t even had the chance to get vaccinated — or they were so recently vaccinated that their bodies hadn’t had a chance to produce immunity against the flu.
The county’s flu season started on Sept. 28. But the early start alone, Terashita noted, isn’t an indicator that the season will be more severe.
The rate at which flu tests are coming back positive since the season’s start has been high in the San Francisco Bay Area and moderate in Southern California and the Sacramento Valley. Flu hospital admission rates remain low across California. So far this year, there have been 34 flu-related deaths in the state, according to the state Department of Public Health’s online dashboard .
San Francisco confirmed its first flu death of the season last week . Los Angeles County has not logged any influenza deaths yet this season, Terashita said. In the 2025-26 flu season, the county recorded 126 influenza deaths, a relatively low total, she noted.
Kaiser has seen a recent increase in outpatient visits related to the flu, though flu hospitalizations have not yet risen. If the current trend continues, Hudson expects hospitalizations to spike in the coming weeks.
Health officials say vaccination is the best form of protection against the flu and are urging people to get their shots soon.
Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, a UC San Francisco infectious-disease expert, said people should aim to get the shot ideally before mid-October. For most, he said, the standard flu shot suffices, though he noted there are other options, including a nasal spray version — great for almost anyone with a fear of needles — and higher-dosage shots. The stronger shots have four times the antigen and are approved for those 65 and older.
The current variant, H3N2 subclade K, appears similar to last year’s strain and is included in this year’s vaccine, reducing concern about a major mismatch between the vaccine and the flu strain, Chin-Hong said.
“The ball is in our court because vaccination behavior drives how we tackle the flu,” he said. “This year we have less excuse because the flu vaccine is well-matched in general to ... what has been circulating so far.”
Los Angeles County’s most severe flu season in recent memory was the 2009 pandemic, according to Terashita. That year, the H1N1 virus led to a high number of hospitalizations and deaths around the world, The Times reported at the time.
Flu cases almost disappeared during the COVID-19 pandemic, Terashita said. As people resumed gatherings and eased up on measures including masking and social distancing, the county saw upticks in flu cases in 2024 and 2025.
“We’re just watching and waiting right now” to see how severe the flu season will be, she said, “but it is a good reminder to everyone that it’s a very good thing you can do to protect yourself, which is get the vaccine.”

Happy World Octopus Day!  Every Oct 8, the world celebrates one of the more unusual creatures of the sea. Octopuses are well-known for their eight legs and ability to squirt ink when frightened. They’ve also been known to use tools, a sign of intelligence, and can shape-shift to mimic the colors and texture of their surroundings, an effective way to disappear from both predators and prey.
Mongabay has reported on several octopus discoveries this year, including:
Ancient octopus were apex predators
Modern colossal squid are believed to be the largest invertebrates in the sea, but Mongabay’s Shanna Hanbury recently reported on an even larger ancient octopus species whose fossils were described by Japanese researchers in April 2026.
The Japanese team found a fossilized jawbone from the now-extinct Nanaimoteuthis haggarti. Based on its jaw size, researchers suggest the octopus may have reached 6.6 to 18.6 meters (22 to 61 feet) in length. On the higher end, that’s around two-thirds the size of an adult blue whale, the largest animal to ever exist.
“It suggests that it may have been among the largest invertebrates ever known,” study co-author Yasuhiro Iba, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University in Japan, told Mongabay by email.
They were likely gigantic predators that roamed the late Cretaceous seas between 100 million to 72 million years ago.
A rare look at baby octopuses
From long dead octopus to newly born, Hanbury also reported on baby Argentine octopuses and a rare photo of them.
Patagonian octopus eggs in Puerto Lobos Protected Natural Area in Argentina. Image courtesy of Martin Brogger.
These eggs belong to a small Patagonian octopus ( Octopus tehuelchus ). It’s one of the more common octopus species in the region, but researchers still haven’t been able to determine its global conservation status, although reported catches in Patagonia have declined over the past 50 years.
The black dots inside each egg are the developing eyes of the embryos, indicating that they’re progressing toward hatching. The female octopus of this species often lays her eggs in the shell of an oyster , then guards them fiercely. She even stops eating during this period.
New octopus species are described often , including a blue octopus about the size of a golf ball recently discovered in the Galapagos.
On a deep-sea expedition in 2015, scientists used a remotely operated vehicle to find a golf-ball sized, short-armed blue octopus. In a recent study , they confirmed that it’s new to science, reported Mongabay’s David Brown.
However, questions remain about how the new species, Microeledone galapagensis , makes use of its stubby arms.
“If you gather prey by moving your arms through the sediment (as we think they do), wouldn’t it be better to have longer arms with more suckers than short little arms?” queried lead author Janet Voight.
Banner image: Big blue octopus ( Octopus cyanea ) with a diver in background. Image courtesy of David Fleetham/WWF via naturepl.com.

articles.title_orig: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.title_zh: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.content_orig:
Sailors wave aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier as it returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
CORONADO, Calif. — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.
The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.
Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.
"It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off."
Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.
"It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday."
She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.
Family and friends cheer as the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to Naval Air Station North Island after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Coronado, Calif. Gregory Bull/AP hide caption
Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.
"It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said.
The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."
Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.
Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.
The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.
Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.
Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.
"She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.
It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said.
When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.
Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.
"I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego. Karl Anderson/AP hide caption
Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.
He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.
The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time.
After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.
The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed nearly 3,700 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

The world’s largest wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills is barreling toward a Dec. 2 completion date . Perhaps the only thing that could stop it is a fierce winter storm.
Already, a concrete bridge stretches across 10 lanes of whizzing traffic. Atop that, there’s a lush landscape sewn with 6,000 native plants. Recently, crews completed another overpass over adjacent Agoura Road. A big remaining to-do is to fill in the gap between the freeway and the road — and the freeway to the land to the north — with millions of cubic feet of soil to create a seamless pathway for animals.
The idea behind the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is to provide a lifeline for mountain lions in the Santa Monica Mountains, locked in by traffic and suffering from the effects of inbreeding.
“We’re just hoping El Niño ‘s on our side,” said Beth Pratt, president of the Wildlife Crossing Fund and public face of the project. “I keep saying, ‘Mother Nature, we’re trying to help you. Let’s not throw any more complications our way.’” A super-sized version of the climate pattern is looming, and there’s a good chance Southern California could be doused.
Some rain is not a big deal but flooding would shut down work for safety reasons. At a final construction update held near the crossing Thursday, Robert Rock, lead landscape architect and principal designer for the crossing, explained that the soil in the area is rich in clay and silt. When wet, it gets dangerously slick and slippery.
Heavy precipitation can also derail the soil compaction process, where crews lay down the soil in layers and go over each with a construction vehicle known as a roller. In the distance, workers were busy doing just that as the fierce late morning sun beat down.
“If you’re trying to compact a mud puddle, it wouldn’t really compact, right?” he said at a trailhead off of Agoura Road. “Because if you push that down, the mud just [splats] in either direction.”
In fact, something like that happened amid historic rains in the winter of 2022-23. Construction workers were busy preparing to pour the concrete for the bottom layer of the north wall. But water collected in the trench that was dug for it as they were working to compact the soil.
That pushed back the original completion date of late 2025. Right-wing pundits and politicos in recent months have attacked the project over the delays and a high price tag that’s currently $114 million. A March post in an outlet published by a conservative think tank called it a “bridge to nowhere” and “jobs program for environmentalists.” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy compared it with the state’s long-delayed, budget-busting high-speed train.
Around the time the outrage reached a fever pitch, however, the completion date was announced.
Pratt said “the hate” has worn on her. She’s been called a “fraud,” “retard” and worse, and she’s even afraid to post about the crossing on social media. “Of course we’re still going to celebrate” at the finish line, she said.
At stake is the survival of the Santa Monica Mountains’ isolated, beleaguered mountain lion population, which is listed as threatened. Seth Riley, wildlife branch chief for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, said 41% of documented matings were between close relatives since 2002, the start of an ongoing study of mountain lions in and around the Santa Monicas.
Just a few months ago, the National Park Service caught a young collared male at the western end of the mountain range who had a kinked tail — a sign of inbreeding. It’s not the first such documented deformity but shows the problems persist, Riley said. If the situation gets to the point where their reproduction is affected, modeling has shown there’s “essentially a 100% chance of extinction” within 50 years, he added.
But he doesn’t think it’s too late. The soon-to-open crossing will let the big cats seek mates in the Simi Hills and beyond — and allow fresh blood to travel into their neck of the woods, he said. Genetic diversity is expected to go up, though not overnight.
In the last three weeks, a trail camera stationed close to the south end of the crossing has captured coyotes, deer, a female lion with two big cubs — even as construction churns on next door, said Jeff Sikich, a wildlife biologist at the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
Recently, in the Simi Hills north of the crossing, his team marked three kittens, the first litter for the 3 ½-year-old lion known as P-113.
“These kittens might be — once they grow up and leave mom at roughly around 1½ — one of the first lions to actually use the wildlife crossing,” he said.
